title: Chance, mixing and new species: how whole populations change

summary.text: In one forest in Odisha, many tigers have wide black stripes that almost hide the orange. Scientists have found no wild tigers like this anywhere else, and the dark coat does not seem to help them. So why is it common there? In this lesson you shake beans in a steel tumbler and watch a colour take over a small group by chance alone. You find out how a few travellers keep two groups alike. You also find out how groups that stop mixing become new species.
summary.art: A tiger with very wide black stripes walking through sal forest, with a steel tumbler of dark and pale beans drawn small in one corner.

intro.hook: Natural selection makes useful features common. But some features are common in one place and do no good at all. If nothing chose them, how did they spread?
intro.text: You may already know natural selection. Members whose features suit the place leave more young, so those features spread. That is one way a population changes. This lesson is about three other ways. First you draw beans from a tumbler with your eyes shut, and find out what chance does to a small group. Then you compare a group of 8 with a group of 40. You pass a narrow bottleneck, and read the real case of the black tigers of Similipal. You open a bridge between two islands of beans and send one traveller across in each round. Last, you lay out paper chromosomes and find out how the wheat in a chapati became a new species in one step.
intro.art: A child with her eyes shut, taking one bean out of a steel tumbler, with small bowls of marked and plain beans beside her.

outcomes: By the end I can explain genetic drift, using my results from the Lucky Tumbler Test.
By the end I can explain why chance changes a small population fast and a large one slowly.
By the end I can describe a bottleneck and the founder effect, with one real example of each.
By the end I can explain gene flow, and how a few travellers keep two populations alike.
By the end I can name four kinds of barrier that keep two species from mixing.
By the end I can explain how doubled chromosomes make a new plant species in one step.
By the end I can say what evidence shows that a common feature is useful, and not common by chance.

terms.meaning: A population is all the living beings of one kind who live in one place and can breed with each other.
terms.example: All the tigers of the Similipal forest in Odisha are one population. All the house crows of Kochi are another.
terms.art: A map of one forest with small tiger shapes scattered inside the border.

terms.meaning: A gene is one instruction in DNA. Many genes come in more than one version. Scientists call each version an allele.
terms.example: In tigers, one gene shapes the stripes. One version gives narrow stripes. Another version gives wide stripes that run together.
terms.art: Two short strips of DNA side by side, alike except for one letter, with a narrow-striped and a wide-striped patch of fur beside them.

terms.meaning: The share of a gene version is the fraction of all the copies in a population that are that version. Scientists call it the frequency.
terms.example: If 4 beans out of 8 are dark, the share of dark is 4 out of 8, which is one half.
terms.art: Eight beans in a row, four dark and four pale, with the fraction 4 out of 8 written under them.

terms.meaning: Something happens by chance when nothing about the members decides the result. Nobody can say beforehand which way it will go.
terms.example: When you draw beans with your eyes shut, colour plays no part in which beans you draw.
terms.art: A child with eyes closed reaching into a steel tumbler.

terms.meaning: Genetic drift is a change in the shares of gene versions that happens by chance alone. No version is better than another, yet the shares move.
terms.example: In the Lucky Tumbler Test, nobody chooses by colour. The share of dark beans still moves up and down from round to round.
terms.art: A wobbly line on a chart wandering up and down from a starting point in the middle.

terms.meaning: A gene version is fixed when every member of the population has it. A version is lost when no member has it any more.
terms.example: When all 8 beans in the tumbler are dark, dark is fixed and pale is lost.
terms.art: A tumbler holding eight dark beans, with a single pale bean crossed out beside the tumbler.

terms.meaning: A bottleneck happens when a large population is cut down to a few survivors. The population that grows back comes only from those few.
terms.example: Hunters left about 20 northern elephant seals alive by 1892. All the seals of today descend from them.
terms.art: A bottle on its side with many beans of five kinds inside and only five beans of two kinds rolled out through the narrow neck.

terms.meaning: The founder effect happens when a few members start a new population. The new population has only the gene versions those few carried.
terms.example: If three cats reach an island and one has a bent tail, bent tails can become common there.
terms.art: A small boat reaching an island with three cats aboard, one with a bent tail.

terms.meaning: Inbreeding is breeding between close relatives. In a very small population, every possible mate is a relative.
terms.example: A tiger population of a few dozen, cut off from other forests, has only cousins to choose from.
terms.art: A small family tree whose branches loop back and join each other.

terms.meaning: Gene flow is the movement of gene versions from one population to another. It happens when a member moves and has young in the new place.
terms.example: A young male tiger walks from Kanha to Pench and fathers cubs there. His gene versions have moved with him.
terms.art: Two forest patches joined by a strip of trees, with a tiger walking along the strip.

terms.meaning: A migrant is a member who moves from one population to another and stays to breed.
terms.example: In the Bridge Test, the one bean that crosses to the other island in each round is a migrant.
terms.art: One bean moving along an arrow from one tumbler to another.

terms.meaning: A wildlife corridor is a strip of forest or wild land that joins two larger wild places. Animals use the corridor to move between them.
terms.example: Forest corridors up to about 200 kilometres long join the Kanha and Pench tiger reserves in central India.
terms.art: A long thin band of forest winding between fields and villages to join two large forests.

terms.meaning: Genetic rescue means bringing a few members from another population into a small, inbred one. They bring gene versions the small group had lost.
terms.example: In 1995, eight female pumas from Texas were released among the last Florida panthers.
terms.art: A large cat stepping out of a transport crate into a swampy forest.

terms.meaning: A species is a group of living beings who can breed with each other and have young who can also have young. This meaning works for most animals, though not for all of life.
terms.example: A horse and a donkey can have a mule, but a mule cannot have young. So horses and donkeys are two species.
terms.art: A horse, a donkey and a mule standing in a row.

terms.meaning: Speciation is the forming of a new species. One species becomes two when two of its populations can no longer breed together.
terms.example: Snapping shrimps on the two sides of Panama were one species before the land rose between the two seas.
terms.art: One branch splitting into two branches, each ending in a slightly different shrimp.

terms.meaning: A reproductive barrier is anything that stops two groups from having young together who can breed. It may be a sea, a season, a song or the chromosomes.
terms.example: Two kinds of firefly can live in one field and never mix, because each answers only the flash pattern of their own kind.
terms.art: Two fireflies in a dark field, one giving a single long flash and one giving three short flashes.

terms.meaning: A hybrid is the young of parents from two different species or two very different populations.
terms.example: A mule is a hybrid of a female horse and a male donkey.
terms.art: A mule with a small horse and a small donkey drawn above as the parents.

terms.meaning: Chromosome doubling happens when a cell copies all the chromosomes but does not divide. The new cell has twice as many sets. Scientists call a being with extra sets a polyploid.
terms.example: Bread wheat has six sets of chromosomes, which came from three different wild grasses.
terms.art: Two paper strips becoming four paper strips inside a circle that stands for one cell.

terms.meaning: A neutral change is a change in DNA that makes no difference to how well a living being survives or has young.
terms.example: Many one-letter changes in DNA leave the protein exactly as before. Only chance decides whether such a change spreads.
terms.art: Two strips of DNA letters with one letter different, both pointing to the same protein shape.

explanations.concept: A population is counted in shares, not in single members
explanations.definition: A population changes when the shares of its gene versions change. A share is the fraction of all the copies that are one version.
explanations.description: One tiger never changes her stripes. So to find out how tigers change, scientists do not watch one tiger. They count the gene versions in a whole population. Think of one gene with two versions. Count every copy of that gene in the population, and find what fraction is each version. Those fractions are the shares. If the shares are the same in the next generation, the population has not changed for that gene. If the shares have moved, the population has evolved a little. In 1908 the English mathematician G. H. Hardy and the German doctor Wilhelm Weinberg each showed something important. The shares stay the same if four things hold. The population is very large. No version helps survival. Nobody arrives or leaves. No new mutation appears. Real populations break these rules all the time, so real shares keep moving. This lesson is about what moves them.
examples: In the Lucky Tumbler Test, you begin with 4 dark beans and 4 pale beans. The share of dark is 4 out of 8, which is one half.
Among 12 tigers tested in Similipal, 58 of every 100 copies of the stripe gene were the wide-stripe version. Among 395 wild tigers from other forests, none were.
A population can change a great deal in shares while looking the same from outside. Many gene versions change nothing that we can see.
explanations.art: A pie chart half dark and half pale beside a tumbler of four dark and four pale beans.

explanations.definition: Genetic drift is a change in the shares of gene versions that happens by chance. Nothing about the versions causes it.
explanations.description: In every generation, some members leave many young and some leave none. Sometimes the reason is a feature, and that is natural selection. But often the reason has nothing to do with any feature. A branch falls on one nest and not on the next. A flood takes the eggs on the low bank. One seed lands on rock and another on soil. Now ask why this changes the shares. The members who leave young are only a sample of the population, and a sample rarely matches the whole exactly. So the next generation begins with slightly different shares. Then the same thing happens again, starting from the new shares. Nothing pulls the shares back to where they began, because the population keeps no record of the old numbers. The small changes add up, the way a person wanders who takes each step in a direction picked by a coin. One more thing about the word chance. It does not mean that nothing caused the branch to fall. It means that the cause had nothing to do with the gene versions. The American biologist Sewall Wright worked out the mathematics of this in 1931.
examples: In Four From Eight, you draw 4 beans from 4 dark and 4 pale with your eyes shut. About half the time you do not get 2 and 2.
In the Lucky Tumbler Test, the dark count on one island may go 4, 6, 6, 8. Nobody looked at colour, and dark still took over.

In 1956 Peter Buri kept 107 small populations of fruit flies. Each began with two versions of an eye-colour gene in equal shares. After 19 generations, more than half the populations had lost one version or the other.
explanations.art: Four wobbly lines starting from the same point and wandering off in four different directions.

explanations.concept: Why chance is strong in a small group and weak in a large one
explanations.definition: The smaller a population is, the faster genetic drift changes its shares. In a very large population, drift is slow.
explanations.description: Toss a coin 4 times. Getting 3 heads would not surprise you, and that is three quarters heads. Now toss the coin 400 times. Getting 300 heads would be astonishing. In a big sample the lucky and unlucky results nearly cancel out. In a small sample they do not. A population works the same way. When only 4 members become parents, one lucky dark bean moves the share a long way. When 20 become parents, one lucky bean hardly shows. So a small island can lose a version within a few generations, while a large population keeps both for a very long time. What counts is the number who actually breed. Scientists call this the effective population size, and it is often far smaller than the number of animals you can count. In a herd where only a few males father all the calves, the breeding number is small even if the herd is large.
examples: In the Lucky Tumbler Test, most islands of 8 beans lose one colour within 10 rounds. A group of 40 beans almost never loses a colour in 5 rounds.
A drop of pond water can hold millions of bacteria. In a population that size, drift moves the shares very slowly.
The last wild Asiatic lions all live in and around one forest in Gujarat. A population in one small place is where drift works fastest.
explanations.art: A small tumbler with a steep wobbly line above it and a large bowl with a nearly flat line above it.

explanations.concept: Drift removes variety, and chance does not bring it back
explanations.definition: When drift takes a gene version down to zero, that version is lost from the population. Only a new mutation or a migrant can bring it back.
explanations.description: Watch what happens at the ends of the Lucky Tumbler Test. While an island has both colours, the count can go up or down. Once the island is all dark, every survivor is dark and every young is dark. The count can never move again. So drift has two results that seem opposite. Different islands become different from each other, because each loses different versions. And each island becomes more alike inside, because versions keep dropping out. Variety is what natural selection works with. A population with few versions has less to draw on when the weather, the food or a disease changes. This is one reason a small, cut-off population is at risk even when every member looks healthy.
examples: In made-up results for four islands of 8 beans, two islands ended all dark, one ended all pale and one still had both colours after 10 rounds.
Northern elephant seals now number more than 200,000. Their DNA still shows very little variety, because all of them descend from about 20 seals.
In the Narrow Neck, 40 beans of 5 kinds pass through a bottleneck of 5 survivors. Most often only 3 kinds are left.
explanations.art: A row of four tumblers, two all dark, one all pale and one mixed.

explanations.concept: Bottlenecks: a population squeezed through a few survivors
explanations.definition: A bottleneck is a sharp fall in the size of a population. The few survivors carry only part of the variety that the population had.
explanations.description: A storm, a disease, a drought or hunting can cut a population down to a handful. The survivors are a small sample, so they carry only some of the gene versions. Which versions get through is mostly chance. When the population grows back, its numbers may recover fully, but the lost versions do not return. A bottleneck also leaves relatives breeding with relatives. Many harmful gene versions do no damage when a body has one copy, and do damage only when a body has two. Relatives often carry the same rare version, so their young more often get two copies. That is why inbred populations tend to have more illness and fewer healthy young.
examples: People hunted northern elephant seals for the oil in their fat. By 1892 only about 20 were left. Today there are more than 200,000, all descended from those few.

Around 1775 a typhoon struck Pingelap, a small island in the Pacific Ocean. About 20 people lived through it. Today roughly 1 islander in every 10 or 20 sees no colour at all. Elsewhere this condition is very rare.
By the early 1990s fewer than 30 Florida panthers were left. Many had heart defects and bent tail tips, which are signs of inbreeding.
explanations.art: A crowd of seals of many different shades on one side of a narrow gap, a few seals passing through, and a large crowd of nearly identical seals on the other side.

explanations.concept: The founder effect, and the black tigers of Similipal
explanations.definition: The founder effect is drift at the start of a new or cut-off population. A few founders carry a small sample of gene versions, and a rare version among them can become common.
explanations.description: Similipal is a tiger reserve in Odisha. Many of its tigers have black stripes so wide that they run together and cover much of the orange. In 2021, Vinay Sagar, Uma Ramakrishnan and their team at the National Centre for Biological Sciences in Bengaluru found the cause. It is a change of one letter in a gene called Taqpep. A tiger looks this way only with two copies of the changed version, one from each parent. In Similipal the changed version made up more than half of all the copies they found. Among 395 wild tigers from other forests, the team found no copies at all. Does the dark coat help a tiger in Similipal? The team found no sign that it does. The Similipal tigers are few, and they are cut off from other tiger forests. In such a group a rare version can become common by chance, helped by relatives breeding with relatives. This is the founder effect together with drift.
examples: In the Founders' Boat, 2 beans out of 50 on the mainland are speckled. When a speckled bean is among the 5 founders, speckled beans are at least 5 times more common on the island.
The sample from Similipal was only 12 tigers. So the share of 58 in 100 is a rough figure, and the team said so.
The team first traced the changed version through families of black tigers living in Indian zoos, where the parents of every cub are known.
explanations.art: A tiger with wide merged black stripes beside a tiger with ordinary narrow stripes, in sal forest.

explanations.concept: Gene flow: gene versions travel between populations
explanations.definition: Gene flow is the movement of gene versions from one population into another. It makes populations more alike.
explanations.description: Animals walk, fly and swim. Seeds ride on wind, water and fur. Pollen travels on bees and on the wind. Whenever a traveller has young in the new place, gene versions arrive with them. Gene flow does two things. It brings versions that the population lacked or had lost, so variety goes up. And it makes the two populations more alike, because each now holds some of the other's versions. So gene flow works against drift. Drift pulls populations apart, and gene flow pulls them back together. Notice that a traveller must breed to count. A tiger who crosses a road and is killed before fathering cubs moves no genes.
examples: In the Bridge Test, one island starts all dark and the other all pale. One bean crosses each way in every round. After 8 rounds both islands hold both colours.

Sandeep Sharma and his team studied the DNA of tigers in four reserves of central India. Reserves still joined by forest corridors, such as Kanha and Pench, had kept their gene flow. Reserves that had lost their corridors had not.
Wind carries pollen from one field of maize or bajra to the next. That is gene flow between fields.
explanations.art: Two tumblers joined by a small paper bridge, with one bean crossing in each direction.

explanations.concept: How little mixing is enough, and what genetic rescue can do
explanations.definition: A very small amount of gene flow is enough to stop two populations from drifting far apart. Bringing in a few migrants can restore a small population's lost variety.
explanations.description: You might think many travellers are needed to keep two populations alike. Sewall Wright's mathematics gave a surprising answer. About one breeding migrant in each generation is enough to keep most gene versions present in both populations. This is true for a herd of 50 and for a herd of 5,000. The reason is that drift is slow in a large group, so a large group needs less mixing to stay the same. In 1996 the biologists Scott Mills and Fred Allendorf checked this rule for wildlife managers. They advised between 1 and 10 migrants per generation, because real populations are messier than the mathematics. The same idea can save a population. In 1995, wildlife managers released eight female pumas from Texas among the last Florida panthers. Five of them had kittens. The panthers have since grown from fewer than 30 to somewhere between 120 and 230.
examples: In the Bridge Test, a single bean crossing each way was one eighth of each island. The two islands still came to look alike within about 8 rounds.
After the Texas pumas arrived, Florida panther kittens with mixed parents survived better than kittens without.
Rescue has a risk. If far too many migrants arrive, the gene versions special to the small population could be swamped. In Florida, studies found that this did not happen.
explanations.art: A panther with two kittens in tall swamp grass.

explanations.definition: People can stop gene flow without meaning to. A highway, a canal, a town or a custom can divide one population into several small ones.
explanations.description: A four-lane highway is only a few metres wide, yet many animals will not cross, or die trying. So a road can split one forest population into two, and each half then drifts as a smaller group. National Highway 44 passes through the Pench tiger forests of central India. There the road was built with nine crossings beneath it for animals. Camera traps set by the Wildlife Institute of India in 2019 photographed 18 kinds of wild animals using them, including 11 different tigers. Customs can be barriers too, and humans are animals to whom this applies. In India, many communities have married only within the community for dozens of generations. In 2017 Nathan Nakatsuka, Kumarasamy Thangaraj of the Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology in Hyderabad, David Reich and their team studied the DNA of more than 2,800 people from over 260 groups. They found that 81 groups had each grown from a small number of founders. In such a group, a harmful gene version that is rare elsewhere can be common. Knowing this helps doctors look for those versions early.
examples: A railway line with fences on both sides can separate the frogs of one pond from the frogs of the next.
The nine crossings under National Highway 44 are between 50 and 750 metres wide, so that even shy animals will use them.
The 2017 study found no group that was a separate kind of human. It found small groups within one well-mixed species, each with a few versions made common by the founder effect.
explanations.art: A raised highway on tall pillars with a tiger and a herd of chital walking through the forest underneath.

explanations.concept: From two populations to two species: the barriers that keep them apart
explanations.definition: Two populations have become two species when barriers stop them from having young together who can breed. Scientists call this reproductive isolation.
explanations.description: While two populations exchange migrants, new gene versions spread through both, and they stay one species. Now suppose the gene flow stops, perhaps because a sea or a hot lowland lies between them. Each population then changes by itself, through its own mutations, its own drift and its own selection. No one change is large. But after many thousands of generations the two may differ in ways that matter for breeding. Scientists sort these barriers into two kinds. Some barriers act before mating. The two groups breed in different months, or live in different parts of the same place. Their songs, flashes or scents may differ, so that neither answers the other. Their flowers may fit different visitors. Other barriers act after mating. The hybrid young may die early, or be healthy but unable to have young. Most pairs of species are kept apart by several barriers at once. None of these barriers was built for the purpose. They are side effects of two populations changing separately.
examples: Time: two kinds of fly may breed in the same orchard weeks apart, so they never meet as adults.
Signal: each kind of firefly flashes a pattern of their own. A female answers only the pattern of her kind.
Visitor: one monkeyflower in North America is pink and visited by bees. A close relative is red and visited by hummingbirds. Pollen seldom passes between them.
After mating: a horse has 64 chromosomes and a donkey has 62. Their mule has 63, an odd number that cannot be shared out evenly, so a mule cannot make working egg or sperm cells.
explanations.art: Four small panels: a calendar with two different months circled, two fireflies with different flash patterns, a bee at a pink flower beside a hummingbird at a red flower, and a mule.

explanations.concept: A sea that became land: the snapping shrimps of Panama
explanations.definition: When a barrier forms at a known time, scientists can measure how far the separated populations have moved towards being separate species.
explanations.description: North and South America were once separate, with open sea between them. Slowly the land of Panama rose, and about 3 million years ago it closed the gap. Sea animals on the two sides could no longer meet. The American biologist Nancy Knowlton and her team studied snapping shrimps there, in work published in 1993. They found seven pairs of close relatives, with one member of each pair in the Pacific Ocean and the other in the Caribbean Sea. The team compared the DNA and proteins of each pair. They also put a male from one sea with a female from the other. Snapping shrimps accept a mate of their own kind and fight anyone else. The cross-sea couples fought more, and paired less, than couples from the same sea. So in about 3 million years, one species on each stretch of coast had become two. The pairs were not all equally different, which showed that the sea closed for some shrimps earlier than for others.
examples: The pairs that differed most in DNA were also the least willing to accept each other as mates.

DNA changes that make no difference to survival pile up at a fairly steady rate. So the number of differences between two species tells roughly how long they have been apart. Scientists call this the molecular clock.
The same event that split the sea animals joined the land animals. Animals from the two continents walked across the new land and met.
explanations.art: A map of the narrow land of Panama with a small shrimp drawn in the sea on each side, the two shrimps a little different in colour.

explanations.definition: If two populations that were apart come into contact, three things can happen. They can merge into one, stay fully separate, or form a hybrid zone where they meet.
explanations.description: Barriers do not last for ever. Seas fall, forests spread and rivers change course. What happens next depends on how far the two populations have changed. If they still breed freely and their hybrid young do well, gene flow starts again and the two slowly become one population. If they no longer breed together at all, they live side by side as two species. Often the result lies in between. The two breed where their ranges touch, but the hybrids do a little less well than either parent kind. Then the hybrids stay in a narrow band called a hybrid zone, and the two kinds stay different on each side. One more thing can happen there. If hybrids do poorly, members who choose mates of their own kind leave more young. So selection can make the two kinds choosier over time. Scientists call this reinforcement.
examples: Carrion crows are all black and hooded crows are grey and black. They meet in a narrow band across Europe and have hybrid young there. The band has stayed narrow for as long as people have mapped it.
In the Bridge Test, two islands that had become different grew alike again once beans could cross. That is merging.
Most people living today carry short pieces of Neanderthal DNA. Two human populations that had been apart for a very long time met, and had children together.
explanations.art: A map with black crows on the left, grey and black crows on the right, and a thin band of in-between crows where they meet.

explanations.concept: A new species in one step: doubled chromosomes
explanations.definition: A new plant species can form in a single generation when a hybrid's chromosomes are doubled. The new plant can breed with others like themself, but not with either parent species.
explanations.description: Chromosomes are the long threads of DNA inside a cell, and they come in matching pairs. To make a pollen grain or an egg cell, a plant must separate each pair, so that each new cell gets one of every kind. Now think of a hybrid between two plant species. The hybrid has one set of chromosomes from each parent, and the two sets do not match. With no partners to pair with, the chromosomes are shared out unevenly. Most pollen and egg cells then lack some instructions, and the hybrid has few or no seeds. Sometimes a cell copies all the chromosomes and then fails to divide. Now every chromosome has an exact partner. A plant grown from that cell can make balanced pollen and eggs, and can set seed with others like themself. But a cross back to either parent gives young with unmatched chromosomes again. So the doubled plant is cut off from both parents at once. This is a new species, made in one step. It is common in plants and rare in animals. The description here is simplified, because real chromosomes sometimes pair in more complicated ways.
examples: Bread wheat, the wheat of atta and chapati, has 42 chromosomes in six sets. About 9,000 years ago a farmed wheat with 28 chromosomes crossed with a wild goat grass with 14, and the chromosomes doubled.
Ragi, or finger millet, has four sets of chromosomes, which came from two different wild grasses.

In 1950 the American botanist Marion Ownbey reported two new species of goatsbeard in the states of Washington and Idaho. Their parent species had been brought from Europe only decades before. Each new species had double the chromosomes of the parents.
The bananas we eat have three sets of chromosomes. An odd number cannot be shared out evenly, which is why they have no seeds and are grown from shoots.
explanations.art: A stalk of wheat with three small wild grasses drawn behind, and arrows from the grasses joining at the wheat.

explanations.concept: Can a new species form with no wall at all?
explanations.description: Most new animal species seem to begin with a barrier in space, such as a sea or a mountain range. Can one population split in two while its members still live in the same place? The best-known case is the apple maggot fly of North America. These flies once laid their eggs only in the fruit of wild hawthorn trees. Settlers planted apple trees, and around the middle of the 1800s some flies began to use apples. Apples ripen earlier than hawthorn fruit. Today the apple flies come out earlier in the year, mate on apples and lay on apples. The hawthorn flies do all of this later, on hawthorn. The two groups live in the same countryside and still exchange a few genes. They differ in the shares of several gene versions.
examples: The apple flies and hawthorn flies are not yet two species. Scientists call them host races, which means groups part of the way to being species.
Chromosome doubling in plants is a case of a new species forming with no wall, and nobody disputes that one.

perspectives.who: Ernst Mayr, a German-American biologist, writing from the 1940s onwards
perspectives.explanation: New animal species nearly always need a barrier in space. Without one, gene flow mixes the population again before any split can grow.

perspectives.who: Guy Bush and Jeffrey Feder, American biologists who studied the apple maggot fly
perspectives.explanation: A new food plant can act as a barrier. If flies mate on the plant where they feed, and the two plants fruit at different times, the two groups mostly stop meeting.
Both happen, and the argument is about how often. Some also ask whether the apple flies had help from gene versions that arose long ago in separated populations.

explanations.art: A red apple and a cluster of small red hawthorn fruits side by side, with a small striped-winged fly on each.

explanations.concept: Chance or selection: which has shaped more of life?
explanations.description: Everyone agrees that both drift and natural selection happen. The argument is about how much each has done. It matters most for DNA. When scientists compare the DNA of two species, they find thousands of differences. Are most of those differences useful ones that selection kept? Or did most of them spread by chance? The answer is not the same for every kind of change. For bodies and behaviour that fit a way of life, such as a beak or a wing, selection is the only known cause. For the letters of DNA, the picture is far less settled.
examples: Much of the DNA of animals and plants makes no protein. A changed letter there often changes nothing we can measure.
Different three-letter DNA words can stand for the same building block of a protein. A change from one such word to another leaves the protein the same.

perspectives.who: Ronald Fisher, an English mathematician and biologist, in the 1930s
perspectives.explanation: Populations in nature are large, so chance mostly cancels out. Natural selection decides nearly everything that lasts.

perspectives.who: Motoo Kimura, a Japanese biologist, in 1968
perspectives.explanation: Most changes in DNA make no difference to survival. They spread or vanish by drift alone. Selection matters for the few changes that do make a difference. This is the neutral theory.

perspectives.who: Tomoko Ohta, a Japanese biologist, in 1973
perspectives.explanation: Many changes are neither neutral nor clearly harmful. They are very slightly harmful. In a large population selection removes them. In a small population drift is stronger than such weak selection, and they can spread.

perspectives.who: Some biologists who study whole genomes today
perspectives.explanation: Selection on one gene also drags along the DNA beside that gene. So selection may shape much more of the genome than the neutral theory allows.

explanations.art: A balance scale with a die on one pan and a sieve on the other, and a long strip of DNA letters underneath.

explanations.definition: All living humans belong to one species. Human populations have never been apart long enough, or completely enough, to become different kinds.
explanations.description: People have always walked, sailed, traded and married across distances. So gene flow has run through the whole human species for as long as our species has existed. In 1972 the American biologist Richard Lewontin measured how human variety is spread. He compared gene versions in populations around the world. He found that about 85 parts in 100 of all human variety can be found inside any one population. Only a small part is a difference between one region's people and another's. Later studies of whole genomes agree. Human groups differ in the shares of gene versions, and not in having different genes. One honest point must be added. With many thousands of DNA letters read together, a scientist can usually tell which part of the world most of a person's ancestors lived in. Small differences in shares, added up over many genes, make that possible. But there is no sharp line anywhere, and no group has a gene that makes them a separate kind.
examples: In Which Bowl?, three bowls hold dark and pale beans in slightly different shares. Shown one bean, you can hardly ever tell which bowl the bean came from.
Skin colour changes little by little as you travel from the equator towards the poles. It follows sunlight, and tells almost nothing about a person's other genes.
Two people from the same village can differ more in their DNA than one of them differs from someone on another continent.
explanations.art: Three bowls of mixed dark and pale beans that look nearly the same, with a child holding up one bean and looking puzzled.

explanations.concept: Following the idea further: atoms, the moving Earth and what nobody knows
explanations.description: Follow drift down to the smallest scale. A new gene version begins as a mutation, and a mutation is a change in a few atoms of one DNA letter. Heat makes every atom jiggle. Now and then a letter is in the wrong shape at the moment the DNA is copied, and the wrong partner letter goes in. Radiation from rocks and from space also breaks DNA. In 1963 the Swedish physicist Per-Olov Löwdin proposed something further. A single proton, which is a particle inside the atom, might jump across a pair of DNA letters by a quantum effect called tunnelling, and so cause a mutation. This is an idea that has not been shown in living cells. Now follow gene flow up to the largest scale. The plates of the Earth's crust move a few centimetres a year. Over millions of years they open seas and close them, as in Panama. Ice ages lock water into ice and lower the sea, so that islands join the mainland and part again. So the list of species on Earth depends partly on the slow movement of rock and ice. Some questions are open. Nobody knows how many gene changes it usually takes to make two populations unable to breed. Nobody knows what share of the differences between species came by chance.
examples: Each time one of your cells divides, about 6 billion letter pairs of DNA are copied. A few mistakes get past the cell's checking, so every person is born with some dozens of new mutations.
The land of Panama rose because one plate of the Earth's crust is sliding under another.

perspectives.who: Per-Olov Löwdin, a Swedish physicist, in 1963
perspectives.explanation: Some mutations may begin when a proton tunnels from one DNA letter to its partner. This remains an idea. In physics, such an effect happens whether or not anyone is watching.
Ordinary chemistry is enough to explain nearly all mutations: heat, copying slips, chemicals and radiation.

explanations.art: Three stacked panels: a pair of DNA letters with one tiny particle hopping between them, a globe with arrows on moving plates, and two islands joined by a strip of land at low sea level.

agreed.text: Chance alone can change the shares of gene versions in a population, and it has been measured.
agreed.evidence: In 1956 Peter Buri kept 107 small populations of fruit flies for 19 generations. Each began with two versions of an eye-colour gene in equal shares. The shares wandered differently in every bottle, and more than half the bottles lost one version.

agreed.text: Drift is faster in small populations than in large ones.
agreed.evidence: The mathematics was worked out by Sewall Wright in 1931, and experiments with flies and bacteria give the results he predicted. You can check it at home with 8 beans and with 40 beans.

agreed.text: A population that has passed through a bottleneck has less genetic variety, even after its numbers recover.
agreed.evidence: Northern elephant seals fell to about 20 animals by 1892. A study of their DNA in 2024 compared old museum specimens with living seals. The living seals had far less variety.

agreed.text: Gene flow makes populations more alike, and a little of it is enough.
agreed.evidence: Tigers in central Indian reserves that are still joined by forest share more gene versions than tigers in reserves that have been cut off. Florida panthers regained variety after eight pumas were brought from Texas.

agreed.text: New species form when populations stop exchanging genes for long enough.
agreed.evidence: Seven pairs of snapping shrimp species sit on opposite sides of Panama, which closed about 3 million years ago. Members of a pair from opposite seas are far less willing to accept each other as mates.

agreed.text: In plants, a new species can form in one generation by chromosome doubling.
agreed.evidence: Scientists can count the chromosomes. Bread wheat has 42, in six sets that match three different wild grasses. Two new goatsbeard species appeared in North America within a few decades, and scientists have since remade them by crossing the parents.

challenging.claim: Every feature of a living being is there because it helps.
challenging.who: A common habit of thought among biologists and everyone else. Stephen Jay Gould and Richard Lewontin argued against it in a well-known paper of 1979.
challenging.for: Many features clearly do help, such as a deep beak for hard seeds. Asking 'what is this for?' has led to many discoveries.
challenging.against: Buri's flies and the black tigers of Similipal show that a version can become common with no help from selection. Some features are side effects of others. A claim that a feature helps needs its own evidence.
challenging.context: This card is about whether everything in a living body has a use. As a rule with no exceptions, the claim has been shown wrong.

challenging.claim: Wild populations are so large that drift hardly matters.
challenging.who: Ronald Fisher, an English mathematician and biologist, in the 1930s
challenging.for: In a truly huge population, chance effects nearly cancel out, and even a small advantage wins in the end.
challenging.against: Many species live as small, partly separate groups. Bottlenecks happen. The number that breed is often far below the number alive.
challenging.context: This card is about how much chance matters in nature. Scientists agree on the mathematics and still argue about real populations.

challenging.claim: Most of the DNA differences between species spread by chance, without helping or harming.
challenging.who: Motoo Kimura, a Japanese biologist, in 1968. Tomoko Ohta added very slightly harmful changes in 1973.
challenging.for: DNA changes that leave a protein unchanged pile up faster than changes that alter the protein. That is what you would expect if most changes that spread are harmless ones.
challenging.against: Some whole-genome studies find signs that selection has touched much of the DNA, at least in species with very large populations.
challenging.context: This card is about the neutral theory, which says that chance explains most change in DNA.

challenging.claim: Animals cannot split into two species unless a sea, a mountain range or some other wall divides them.
challenging.who: Ernst Mayr, a German-American biologist, from the 1940s
challenging.for: Nearly every well-studied pair of young animal species has a barrier in space in their history.
challenging.against: Apple maggot flies are dividing in the same orchards, by food plant and season. Fishes in some small crater lakes appear to have split with no barrier.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a new species can form while its members still live in the same place.

challenging.claim: Hybrids are dead ends and play no part in evolution.
challenging.who: Many zoologists for much of the 1900s
challenging.for: Many hybrids, such as mules, cannot have young.
challenging.against: Bread wheat, ragi and many other plants began as hybrids. Most people alive carry DNA from Neanderthals. Gene versions do sometimes pass between species through hybrids who can breed.
challenging.context: This card is about hybrids, who are the young of two different species. The old view that they never matter has been shown wrong.

challenging.claim: A rare population should always be kept pure, and never mixed with outsiders.
challenging.who: Many conservation workers, especially before the 1990s
challenging.for: A local population may have features suited to the place. Too many outsiders could swamp those features.
challenging.against: Florida panthers were dying out from inbreeding until eight pumas from Texas were added. In late 2024 two tigresses from Maharashtra were moved to Similipal to add variety there.
challenging.context: This card is about whether people should move animals between populations to add lost gene versions.

big_questions.q: In the Lucky Tumbler Test, a colour took over without being better. How could you ever prove that a real feature is useful?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you would have to measure. Would it be enough to show that the feature is common?

big_questions.q: If the history of one island were run again from the same start, would the same version win?
big_questions.hint: Look at your four islands. They all started the same.

big_questions.q: Two populations become two species slowly. Is there a first day on which they are two?
big_questions.hint: Think of the apple flies and the hawthorn flies. What would you call them today?

big_questions.q: Is 'species' something in nature, or a word people use to sort what they see?
big_questions.hint: A firefly answers only her own kind's flashes. Yet scientists argue over where to draw many lines.

big_questions.q: Much about you was settled by chance: which egg, which sperm, which ancestors met. Does that make it matter less?
big_questions.hint: Think about whether a thing must have a reason behind it to be valued.

big_questions.q: People build roads that split populations. Do we owe other animals a way across?
big_questions.hint: Think about who gains from the road, and who pays for it.

big_questions.q: Human groups differ only in the shares of gene versions. Why do people so often treat groups as different kinds?
big_questions.hint: Think about the Which Bowl? activity. What can one bean tell you about the bowl?

story.title: The Cats of the Thuruthu
story.note: The island, Nila, Ammachi, Saramma, Thankamma and the cats are all made up, and so are the counts. These things are real. Vembanad Lake in Kerala has many small islands that can be reached only by boat, and 'thuruthu' is a Malayalam word for such an island. Coir rope is made from coconut husk, and rats do gnaw it. Bent or kinked tails in cats are inherited. A study of Asian cats in 2016 found that a kitten with a kinked tail always had at least one parent with a kinked tail.
text: The ferry to the thuruthu was a long black canoe, and the woman who poled it never hurried. Nila sat in the middle with her school bag on her knees. Kochi was two buses behind her. Ahead was Ammachi's island, which had forty houses, one shop and no road.
A cat was waiting on the landing stone. She was the colour of milky tea, and her tail had a bend near the tip, like a finger beckoning.

By the end of the first week, Nila had noticed something. The cat at the shop had the same bend. So did the black cat who slept in Ammachi's woodpile, and the three kittens under the church steps. At home in Kochi, Nila fed four cats behind the flats, and every one of them had a tail as straight as a ruler.
"Why do the cats here have bent tails?" she asked Saramma, who sold fish from a basket.
"For the boats," said Saramma at once. "A cat on a canoe edge needs a hook to balance with."
She asked the teacher at the one-room school. "The lake wind," he said. "It blows from the west all year. Things grow the way the wind pushes them."
She asked her cousin Appu. "They get them shut in doors," said Appu, who had once shut his own finger in one.
That made three reasons, and Nila did not see how all three could be right. She took a notebook and walked the whole island, which took an hour. She counted twenty-three cats. Seventeen had the bend.
Then she tested the reasons, one at a time.
The kittens under the church steps were ten days old. Their eyes were barely open, and they had never met a door. Two of the three had the bend already. Nila crossed out Appu's reason.
A white cat near the coconut sheds had a straight tail. She had lived on the island all her life, in the same west wind. Nila crossed out the teacher's reason.

The boats took longer. For three evenings Nila sat on the landing stone and watched the cats come down for fish scraps. They walked along the canoe edges, bent tails and straight tails alike. In three evenings one cat fell in. She had a bend.
Nila crossed out the last reason and looked at her page. Seventeen out of twenty-three, and no reason left.
On the day before she went home, the ferry woman was mending a pole on the bank. Her name was Thankamma. She was older than Ammachi, and she had poled the canoe before the school was built.
"You have been counting our cats," Thankamma said. "Saramma told me. What did you find?"
"That the bend isn't for anything," said Nila. "But it's nearly everywhere. So there must be a reason I haven't thought of."

Thankamma pushed a peg into the pole with her thumb. "When my mother came here as a bride, there was not one cat on the thuruthu. There were rats. They ate the rice, and they chewed the coir rope the whole island lived on. So my mother went to the market in Alappuzha and came back with a fish basket. There were three kittens in it. Two sisters and a brother."
She held up one finger and crooked the top of it.
"The brother had a tail like this. We called him Kokki, the hook. Nobody chose him for it. He was what was in the basket."
Nila looked along the bank. The tea-coloured cat sat on the landing stone, washing a paw. Beyond her, a black cat was walking the edge of a canoe.
"All of them?" she said. "All twenty-three?"
"Where else would a cat come from? Cats do not swim the lake." Thankamma laughed. "If the basket had held a different brother, you would have had nothing to count."
Nila opened the notebook. Under the three crossed-out reasons she wrote one line: Three kittens in a basket, and one was Kokki.
It did not look like a reason. It looked like something that had happened once, on one day, and had never stopped mattering.

The next morning the canoe took her back across. The tea-coloured cat rode as far as the middle of the lake on the front of the boat, the way she always did. Then she turned round, and Nila could see the small bend near the tip of her tail.
story.epiphany: For the parent: this is the founder effect. Every cat on the island descends from three kittens, so the island's cats hold only the gene versions those three carried. One founder had a bent tail, which is inherited. In so small a group, chance alone could make his version common. The bend does not help a cat. Nila's three tests ruled out the useful-sounding reasons one by one, and that is how a scientist tells a useful feature from one that is common by chance. The cause was not something the bend does. It was who happened to arrive.
ask: Why might a feature be common in a small, cut-off group even if the feature does nothing?
How could you test whether a feature helps the animals who have it?
Suppose three different kittens had started a population. Would it look the same today?
People gave three reasons at once, with no evidence. Why do we so quickly invent a reason for what we see?

games.title: What Changed the Shares? The cause cards
games.context: This is a card game about the four things that change a population: mutation, natural selection, genetic drift and gene flow. Each card tells a real or home-test case. You say which of the four did it.

printables.title: 20 case cards to cut out (the cause is on the back)

items.f: In one small forest in Odisha, wide black stripes are common in tigers. The dark coat does not seem to help.
items.b: Genetic drift, with the founder effect. The tigers are few and cut off, so a rare version became common by chance.

items.f: After a drought left only hard seeds, the finches of one island had deeper beaks on average.
items.b: Natural selection. Deep beaks cracked the hard seeds, so those birds lived and had chicks.

items.f: Northern elephant seals number over 200,000, yet their DNA has very little variety.
items.b: Genetic drift, through a bottleneck. All of them descend from about 20 survivors of hunting.

items.f: Florida panther kittens became healthier after eight pumas from Texas were released among the panthers.
items.b: Gene flow. The pumas brought gene versions that the small panther population had lost.

items.f: A poison killed most mosquitoes. Some years later, the same poison killed very few.
items.b: Natural selection. The few who could survive the poison had young, who inherited that ability.

items.f: On one Pacific island, about 1 person in 10 or 20 sees no colour. Elsewhere this is very rare.
items.b: Genetic drift, through a bottleneck. About 20 people lived through a typhoon, and one carried the version.

items.f: Tigers in Kanha and Pench, two forests joined by a corridor, share most of their gene versions.
items.b: Gene flow. Tigers walk the corridor and have cubs at the other end.

items.f: When a bacterium copies their DNA, one letter is copied wrongly. A version exists that never existed before.
items.b: Mutation. Every new gene version begins as a copying mistake or as damage to DNA.

items.f: A scientist kept 107 small bottles of flies. In more than half, one version of a gene vanished in 19 generations.
items.b: Genetic drift. The versions did not differ in survival. Chance decided which flies were parents.

items.f: On a dark cloth, a hunter picks up the beans she sees first. After three hunts the beans are mostly dark.
items.b: Natural selection. Pale beans were easier to see, so more dark beans survived to have young.

items.f: Your maize has yellow grains. Your neighbour grows red maize. This year a few of your cobs have red grains.
items.b: Gene flow. Wind carried pollen from the neighbour's field to yours.

items.f: A hybrid grass copies all the chromosomes in one cell but the cell does not divide. The new plant has double the number.
items.b: Mutation, and a very large one. Chromosome doubling can make a new plant species in one step.

items.f: You draw beans from a tumbler with your eyes shut. After six rounds every bean in the tumbler is pale.
items.b: Genetic drift. Nobody chose by colour. In a group of 8, chance moves the shares fast.

items.f: Hunters killed elephants with tusks for many years. Afterwards, more females were born without tusks.
items.b: Natural selection. Tuskless females were not hunted, so they lived to have calves.

items.f: A community has married only within the community for many generations. A rare illness is common in it.
items.b: Genetic drift, with the founder effect. The community grew from few founders, and one carried that version.

items.f: A medicine kills nearly all the bacteria in a wound. The few left multiply, and the medicine no longer works.
items.b: Natural selection. Only bacteria who could survive the medicine were left to multiply.

items.f: Radiation from a rock changes one letter in the DNA of a seed.
items.b: Mutation. Radiation, heat and chemicals can all damage DNA and change a letter.

items.f: All-black crows and grey-and-black crows have hybrid chicks in a narrow band where their ranges meet.
items.b: Gene flow, but only a little. The two kinds stay different on each side of the band.

items.f: One island of beans is all dark and another is all pale. One bean crosses each way in every round. Soon both islands hold both colours.
items.b: Gene flow. Each traveller carries a colour to the island that lacked it.

items.f: Three cats are taken to an island with no cats. One has a bent tail. Years later most cats there have bent tails.
items.b: Genetic drift, with the founder effect. The bend became common because of who arrived, and not because it helps.

printables.title: Score sheet
items: One row for each player. Make a mark for every card you keep.

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, case side up.
On your turn, read the top card aloud. Say which cause changed the population: mutation, natural selection, genetic drift or gene flow.
Give your reason in one sentence. Then turn the card over.
If you named the cause, keep the card. If not, put the card at the bottom of the pile.
The game ends when the pile is finished. The player with the most cards wins.
Playing alone: try to keep 15 of the 20 cards on the first time through.

flow.say: Four things change a population. Mutation makes a new version. Selection, drift and gene flow change the shares. Each card is a case of one of them.

ask.q: How can you tell drift from selection in a card?
good: In selection, the feature changes who survives or has young.
In drift, the feature makes no difference and the group is small.

flow.parent: The hardest pair is drift and selection. Ask one question each time: does the card say that the feature helped anyone survive? If the card says the group was small and the feature did nothing, the cause is drift.

flow.say: Sort the cards into four piles. Which of the four causes makes two populations more alike? Which ones make them more different?
flow.kid: Count your cards. Sort all the cards into four piles by cause.

check.q: Which of these makes two populations more alike?
options: Gene flow
Genetic drift
A new mutation in one of them
check.why: Gene flow carries versions from each population into the other, so their shares move closer. Drift moves each population in a direction of their own, so they grow apart. If you chose drift, look at your four islands in the Lucky Tumbler Test: they began alike and ended different.

flow.parent: The piles come out as 3 mutation, 5 selection, 7 drift and 5 gene flow.
flow.context: This is the last step of What Changed the Shares? Here you sort the case cards by cause.

games.title: Kept Apart: a memory game about what separates species
games.context: This is a memory game about reproductive barriers. A barrier is anything that stops two groups from having young together who can breed. You match each barrier to a real example.

printables.title: 16 cards to cut out: 8 barriers and 8 examples
items: BARRIER: land rises and divides one sea into two.
EXAMPLE: snapping shrimps on the two sides of Panama. A pair from opposite seas seldom accept each other as mates.
BARRIER: hot low land lies between two cool hilltops.
EXAMPLE: one small songbird lives north of the Palghat Gap in the Western Ghats, and a close relative lives south of it.
BARRIER: the two groups breed at different times of the year.
EXAMPLE: apple flies come out and mate weeks before hawthorn flies, in the same countryside.
BARRIER: the two groups signal with different patterns of light.
EXAMPLE: each kind of firefly answers only the flash pattern of their own kind.
BARRIER: the two groups sing different songs.
EXAMPLE: two kinds of cricket look alike, but a female comes only to the chirp of her own kind.
BARRIER: different animals carry the pollen of each group.
EXAMPLE: a pink monkeyflower is visited by bees, and a red monkeyflower by hummingbirds.
BARRIER: the two can have young together, but those young cannot have young.
EXAMPLE: a horse and a donkey have a mule, who has 63 chromosomes.
BARRIER: one group has double the number of chromosome sets.
EXAMPLE: bread wheat has six sets of chromosomes and cannot breed with the wild grasses they came from.

rules: Shuffle the 16 cards and lay them face down in four rows of four.
On your turn, turn over two cards and read them aloud.
If one is a barrier and the other is the example of that barrier, say how the barrier stops the two groups from mixing. Then keep the pair and take another turn.
If they do not match, turn them face down again in the same places.
The game ends when all 8 pairs are found. The player with the most pairs wins.
Playing alone: count your turns. Try to finish in 20 turns or fewer, then try to beat your own count.

setup.caption: 3. If they match, say how the barrier works and keep the pair.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 16 cards. 2. Shuffle them. 3. Lay them face down in four rows of four.
flow.say: Eight cards name a barrier. Eight cards give a real example. Each barrier has one example somewhere on the table.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and mix them. Lay them face down in four rows.
flow.context: This is the first step of Kept Apart. Here you lay out the 16 cards.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to turn over two cards. 2. Read both aloud. 3. If they match, say how the barrier works before keeping the pair.
flow.say: Read both cards. Is one the example of the other? Tell me how this barrier keeps the two groups from mixing.
flow.kid: Turn over two cards and read them. Do they match? Say how the barrier works.

ask.q: Which barriers act before two animals ever mate, and which act afterwards?
good: Place, season, light signals, songs and pollen carriers act before.
The mule and the doubled chromosomes act afterwards, on the young.

flow.parent: If your child matches a pair from memory, ask for the explanation before they keep it. The explanation is the point of the game.
flow.context: This is the main part of Kept Apart. Here you look for a barrier and its real example.

flow.do: 1. Count the pairs. 2. Lay the 8 barrier cards in a row. 3. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Look at the eight barriers. Did any animal or plant make a barrier in order to become a new species?
flow.kid: Count your pairs. Lay the 8 barriers in a row. Did anyone plan them?

check.q: Why do reproductive barriers appear between two separated populations?
options: As side effects of each changing separately
Because each wants to be a new species
Because a scientist names them differently
check.why: Each population changes through its own mutations, drift and selection. Some of those changes happen to affect season, signals or chromosomes, and so breeding. If you chose 'each wants to be a new species', remember that these changes built up while the two groups never met. A species is also not made by naming. The name comes after the barrier.

flow.parent: A good answer says that nobody planned the barriers. They built up while the groups were apart.
flow.context: This is the last step of Kept Apart. Here you think about where the barriers came from.

experiments.title: The Lucky Tumbler Test: when nobody chooses, do the colours stay half and half?
experiments.question: An island holds 8 beans, 4 dark and 4 pale. In every round, 4 beans picked with your eyes shut leave no young, and the other 4 each have one young. Nobody looks at colour. After 10 rounds, is the island still half dark and half pale? Do four islands end the same? Does a group of 40 behave like a group of 8?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. After 10 rounds, how many of the 8 beans on one island will be dark? Will four islands that start the same end the same? Will a group of 40 change more, less or the same as a group of 8? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every island starts with 4 dark and 4 pale beans. The beans are the same kind, so fingers cannot tell them apart. The picker's eyes stay shut. In every round exactly half the beans are taken out, and every bean left gets one young of the same colour. Only chance differs between islands. For the last part, only the size of the group changes.
results_table: Island A: dark beans out of 8
Big group: dark beans out of 40

materials.item: pale dry beans, all of one kind, such as white karamani (lobia), kabuli chana or white rajma
a permanent marker or a dark sketch pen, to colour 40 of the beans
a steel tumbler
a deep bowl or a dabba, and a cloth to cover it, for the group of 40
small bowls for the spare dark beans and the spare pale beans
a notebook, a pencil and a ruler

experiments.safety: Dry beans are a choking risk for children under three. Pick up any that fall on the floor.
experiments.record: Draw a table with a row for the start and for rounds 1 to 10. Make one column for each island. Write the number of dark beans after every round. Add a last column for the group of 40, for rounds 1 to 5.
experiments.context: In this experiment, beans in a steel tumbler stand for a small population on an island. You take out half of them in each round with your eyes shut, so nothing but chance decides who has young. Then you count how the colours change.
