setup.caption: 3. With eyes shut, take out 4 beans. They leave no young.

setup.art: Four beans tipped onto the table, three dark and one pale, with a matching new bean being placed beside each.
setup.caption: 4. Give each bean that is left one young of the same colour.

setup.art: A notebook table with columns for Islands A to D and a child writing the number 6 in one box.
setup.caption: 5. Write the number of dark beans. Do 10 rounds for each island.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: number of dark beans

flow.do: 1. Show your child the tumbler and the beans. 2. Explain one round, using the steps in the pictures. 3. Ask for the three guesses and a reason for each. Write them down.
flow.say: Nobody will look at colour in this test. After ten rounds, how many of the eight beans will be dark? Will four islands end the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how many beans will be dark after 10 rounds. Will four islands end the same? Say why.

ask.q: Why do you think the colours will stay at 4 and 4, or move away from it?
good: Nobody is choosing, so it should stay half and half.
With eyes shut I might take more of one colour just by luck.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most children, and most adults, say the island will stay close to 4 and 4 because nothing favours either colour.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Lucky Tumbler Test. You guess what chance alone will do to a small group of beans.

flow.do: 1. Colour 40 beans all over with the marker. Leave them to dry for two minutes. 2. Put the dark beans in one small bowl and 40 pale beans in the other. 3. Draw the results table.
flow.say: The dark beans and the pale beans must feel exactly the same. Why does that matter, if your eyes are shut?
flow.kid: Colour 40 beans dark and let them dry. Put dark and pale in two bowls. Draw the table.
flow.parent: If you have red and white karamani of the same size, use those and skip the colouring. Do not mix two kinds of bean that feel different, such as kala chana and kabuli chana. Fingers would learn to choose.
flow.context: In this step of the Lucky Tumbler Test you make dark and pale beans that feel the same.

flow.do: 1. Put 4 dark and 4 pale beans in the tumbler. This is Island A. 2. Cover the tumbler and shake. 3. With eyes shut, your child takes out 4 beans, one at a time. 4. Tip out the 4 beans left. Add one bean of the same colour for each. 5. Write the number of dark beans. Put all 8 back and do round 2.
flow.say: Shake, shut your eyes and take out four. Those four leave no young. Each bean left has one young of the same colour. How many dark beans now?
flow.kid: Shake the tumbler. Shut your eyes and take out 4 beans. Give each bean left one young. Write the dark count.

check.q: In the Lucky Tumbler Test, what decides which beans leave no young?
options: Chance alone
Their colour
Their size
check.why: Your eyes are shut and the beans feel the same, so nothing about a bean decides whether you take that bean. If you chose colour, that would be natural selection, as when a hunter sees pale beans on a dark cloth. Here no feature matters.

flow.parent: The number of dark beans after a round is always even, because every bean left is doubled. Carry on to round 10. If the island becomes all one colour, write that number down to round 10 and stop, because it can no longer change.
flow.context: In this step of the Lucky Tumbler Test you run the first island of 8 beans for up to 10 rounds.

flow.do: 1. Start Island B with 4 dark and 4 pale beans. Run up to 10 rounds, as before. 2. Do the same for Island C and Island D. 3. Write every count in the table.
flow.say: Island B starts exactly as Island A did. Do you expect the same numbers? Let's see.
flow.kid: Start again with 4 dark and 4 pale. Do 10 rounds. Then do two more islands.
flow.parent: One round takes about half a minute once you have the rhythm. A second person can run a second tumbler to save time. Expect about three of your four islands to end all dark or all pale. Which colour wins on each is as hard to call as a coin toss.
flow.context: In this step of the Lucky Tumbler Test you run three more islands that start exactly the same.

flow.do: 1. Put 20 dark and 20 pale beans in the deep bowl and cover it with the cloth. 2. Stir with a hand under the cloth. 3. With eyes shut, your child takes out 20 beans, counting aloud. 4. Sort the 20 beans left by colour and add a matching young for each. 5. Write the number of dark beans out of 40. Do 5 rounds.
flow.say: This group is five times bigger. Half still leave no young in every round. Will its dark share move as far as the small islands did?
flow.kid: Put 20 dark and 20 pale in the bowl. Take out 20 with eyes shut. Double the rest. Do 5 rounds.
flow.parent: To compare fairly, look at shares. On an island, 6 dark out of 8 is three quarters. In the big group, 22 out of 40 is just over half. The big group nearly always stays between 10 and 30 dark beans, and it does not lose a colour in 5 rounds.
flow.context: In this step of the Lucky Tumbler Test you run a group of 40 beans to compare with the islands of 8.

flow.do: 1. Draw a line chart. Put rounds 0 to 10 along the bottom and dark beans, 0 to 8, up the side. 2. Draw one line for each island, in four colours. 3. Mark where any line reaches 0 or 8.
flow.say: All four lines start at four. Draw each island's line. What happens to a line once it touches the top or the bottom?
flow.kid: Draw a line chart with one line for each island. All four start at 4.
flow.parent: A line that reaches 0 or 8 stays there. That flat end is the most important thing on the chart.
flow.context: In this step of the Lucky Tumbler Test you draw a line chart of the dark beans on each island.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table and the chart together. 2. Ask your child what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. 3. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened. Was either colour better at anything?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: No colour was better. So why did some islands end with only one colour?
good: By luck, more of one colour were left in some rounds.
The next round started from the new numbers, so the luck added up.
Once a colour reached zero there was nobody to bring it back.

ask.q: Why did the group of 40 change less than the islands of 8?
good: With 20 parents, the lucky and unlucky ones nearly cancel.
One bean is a big part of 8 and a small part of 40.

flow.parent: The reason: the 4 beans left in each round are a small sample, and a small sample rarely matches the whole. So the share of dark moves a little in each round, and nothing moves it back. The changes add up until one colour is gone. This is genetic drift. It is change without selection. The model leaves things out. Real parents have different numbers of young. Real populations change size. New versions appear by mutation and arrive with migrants. If all four of your islands still have both colours after 10 rounds, that is unusual and also a fair result. Run five more rounds and watch.
flow.think: If a visitor saw only your all-dark island, what wrong story might they tell about dark beans?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Lucky Tumbler Test. You say what your counts show about chance in small and large groups.

experiments.title: The Bridge Test: can one traveller in each round keep two islands alike?
experiments.question: East Island has 8 dark beans. West Island has 8 pale beans. In every round, one bean picked with your eyes shut crosses from each island to the other. Is one traveller out of 8 enough to make the islands alike? What happens when the bridge is closed again?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. After 8 rounds with one bean crossing each way, how many dark beans will East Island have? How many will West Island have? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both islands always hold 8 beans. In every round, each island loses 4 beans picked with eyes shut, and the 4 left are doubled, as in the Lucky Tumbler Test. The only thing that changes between the parts of the test is whether a bean crosses the bridge.
results_table: East Island: dark beans out of 8
West Island: dark beans out of 8

materials.item: the dark and pale beans from the Lucky Tumbler Test
steel tumblers, one for each island
small bowls for spare beans
a strip of paper to lay between the tumblers as the bridge
a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: Dry beans are a choking risk for children under three. Pick up any that fall on the floor.
experiments.record: Draw a table with a row for the start and for each round. Write the number of dark beans on each island, and the difference between the two numbers.
experiments.context: In the Lucky Tumbler Test, islands that started the same drifted apart by chance. In this experiment two islands start completely different. You send one bean across in each round and find out whether that small amount of mixing makes them alike.

setup.art: Two steel tumblers side by side, the left one full of dark beans and the right one full of pale beans, with a paper strip lying between them as a bridge.
setup.caption: 1. East Island has 8 dark beans. West Island has 8 pale beans.

setup.art: A child with eyes shut taking beans out of one tumbler, with matching new beans being added beside the ones left.
setup.caption: 2. On each island, take out 4 with eyes shut. Double the 4 left.

setup.art: Two hands, each holding one bean, crossing over the paper bridge in opposite directions.
setup.caption: 3. With eyes shut, take one bean from each island and swap them.

setup.art: A notebook table with columns for East Island, West Island and the difference.
setup.caption: 4. Write the dark count on each island. Do 8 rounds.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results with the bridge open

flow.do: 1. Put 8 dark beans in one tumbler and 8 pale beans in the other. 2. Lay the paper strip between them. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write them down.
flow.say: These islands are as different as they can be. One bean will cross each way in every round. After eight rounds, how many dark beans on each island? Why?
flow.kid: One island is all dark. One is all pale. Guess the dark count on each after 8 rounds. Say why.
flow.parent: Many children say one traveller is too few to matter, so East Island will still be nearly all dark. Write the guess down.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Bridge Test. You guess what one traveller in each round will do to two different islands.

flow.do: 1. Take the paper bridge away. 2. Run two rounds on each island, as in the Lucky Tumbler Test. 3. Write the dark counts.
flow.say: The bridge is closed. Take out four and double the rest, on each island. Did anything change? Could it ever change?
flow.kid: Close the bridge. Do 2 rounds on each island. Did anything change?
flow.parent: Nothing can change. East Island has only dark beans to double, and West Island has only pale. Without mutation or a migrant, a lost colour stays lost.
flow.context: In this step of the Bridge Test you run both islands with no bean crossing.

flow.do: 1. Put the bridge back. 2. On each island, take out 4 beans with eyes shut and double the 4 left. 3. Shake both tumblers. With eyes shut, take one bean from each and swap them. 4. Write the dark count on each island and the difference. 5. Do 8 rounds.
flow.say: First the islands lose four and double the rest. Then one bean crosses each way. What is the difference between the islands now?
flow.kid: Take out 4 on each island and double the rest. Swap one bean. Write both counts. Do 8 rounds.

check.q: In the Bridge Test, what does the bean that crosses to the other island stand for?
options: An animal who moves and has young in the new place
A mutation
An animal who dies
check.why: The bean joins the other island and is doubled there in later rounds, so their colour is passed on. That is gene flow. If you chose mutation, remember that a mutation makes a version that did not exist before. The traveller carries a version that already existed elsewhere.

flow.parent: Count after the swap, so the number can be odd. The difference usually falls from 8 to about 2 within 8 rounds. Sometimes both islands end all dark or all pale together. That is the two islands drifting as one group of 16.
flow.context: In this step of the Bridge Test you send one bean across in each round and count the dark beans on each island.

flow.do: 1. Take the bridge away again. 2. Run 5 more rounds on each island with no swap. 3. Write the counts and the difference.
flow.say: The bridge is closed again. The islands are now alike. Will they stay alike with no travellers?
flow.kid: Close the bridge again. Do 5 more rounds. Do the islands stay alike?
flow.parent: With no bean crossing, each island drifts in a direction of their own, as in the Lucky Tumbler Test. In many homes the difference grows again within 5 rounds. If it does not, look at whether either island has lost a colour.
flow.context: In this step of the Bridge Test you close the bridge and watch the two islands again.

flow.do: 1. Look at the difference column for all three parts. 2. Ask your child what they guessed, what they saw and why they think it happened. 3. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Say what you guessed, what you saw and why you think it happened. What would these islands need in order to become two species?
flow.kid: Say what you guessed. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: One bean is only one eighth of an island. Why did it change so much?
good: The traveller was doubled in later rounds.
A new traveller arrived in every round, so they added up.
It brought a colour the island did not have at all.

ask.q: What must happen before two populations can become two species?
good: They must stay apart for a very long time.

flow.parent: The reason: each traveller brings a version to the island that lacked it, and that version is then copied there. A new traveller arrives in every round. So the two islands move towards the same shares. This is gene flow. It works against drift. Sewall Wright showed that about one breeding migrant per generation is enough to keep two populations from drifting far apart. For two populations to become two species, gene flow must stop, or nearly stop, for a very long time.
flow.think: A highway is built between two forests. What has happened to the bridge?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Bridge Test. You say what your counts show about mixing between two groups.

activities.title: Four From Eight: does a blind handful match the whole?
activities.context: In this activity you draw 4 beans from a tumbler of 4 dark and 4 pale, with your eyes shut. You do this ten times and count how often you get exactly 2 of each.

materials.item: pale beans of one kind, such as white karamani or kabuli chana, with 4 of them coloured dark with a marker
a steel tumbler
a notebook and a pencil

activities.record: Ten rows. In each row write how many of the 4 beans you drew were dark.

setup.art: A steel tumbler with four dark and four pale beans inside, seen from above.
setup.caption: 1. Put 4 dark and 4 pale beans in the tumbler.

setup.art: A child with eyes shut holding four beans in an open palm, three dark and one pale.
setup.caption: 2. Shake. With eyes shut, draw 4 beans. Count the dark ones.

setup.art: A notebook page with ten rows of numbers such as 2, 3, 1, 2, 2, 4.
setup.caption: 3. Put them back. Do this 10 times.

flow.do: 1. Show the 4 dark and 4 pale beans going into the tumbler. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write them down.
flow.say: Half these beans are dark. You will draw four with your eyes shut, ten times. How many times out of ten will you get exactly two dark and two pale? Why?
flow.kid: Half the beans are dark. Guess how often you will draw exactly 2 dark. Say why.
flow.parent: Many children say nine or ten times out of ten, because half the beans are dark.
flow.context: This is the first step of Four From Eight. Here you guess how often a blind handful will match the whole.

flow.do: 1. Shake the tumbler. 2. Your child draws 4 beans with eyes shut. 3. Write how many are dark. 4. Put all 4 back. 5. Do this 10 times.
flow.say: Shake, shut your eyes and draw four. How many dark? Write the number and put them back.
flow.kid: Shake and draw 4 with eyes shut. Write how many are dark. Put them back. Do it 10 times.
flow.parent: Putting the beans back each time keeps every draw the same. Expect exactly 2 dark in about 5 of the 10 draws. Getting it 3 times or 7 times is also quite common.
flow.context: In this step of Four From Eight you draw 4 beans ten times and count the dark ones.

flow.do: 1. Count the draws that gave exactly 2 dark. 2. Compare with the guess. 3. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: How many draws gave exactly two and two? What if the four you drew were the only ones to have young?
flow.kid: Count the draws with exactly 2 dark. Was your guess right?

check.q: A tumbler is half dark beans. You draw 4 with eyes shut. What is most likely true?
options: About half the time you get 2 dark
You always get 2 dark
You never get 4 of one colour
check.why: A small sample often differs from the whole. Exactly 2 dark comes up in about half the draws, and 1 or 3 dark in most of the others. If you chose 'always', look at your ten rows. Four of one colour is rare but possible: it comes up about once in 35 draws.

flow.parent: This is the idea the whole unit rests on: a small sample rarely matches the whole exactly. In the Lucky Tumbler Test, the sample becomes the parents of the next round.
flow.context: This is the last step of Four From Eight. Here you compare your ten draws with your guess.

activities.title: The Narrow Neck: what gets through a bottleneck?
activities.context: A bottleneck is a time when a large population is cut down to a few survivors. In this activity 40 seeds of five kinds stand for a population. Only 5 get through, and you find out how many kinds are left.

materials.item: five kinds of dry seed from the kitchen, such as rajma, kabuli chana, kala chana, green moong and groundnuts: 16 of the first, 10 of the second, 8 of the third, 4 of the fourth and 2 of the fifth
a cloth bag, a sock or a deep dabba that you cannot see into
a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: Dry beans and groundnuts are a choking risk for children under three.
activities.record: A table with three rows, one for each try. Write which kinds got through and how many kinds were lost.

setup.art: Five small heaps of different seeds on a newspaper, labelled 16, 10, 8, 4 and 2.
setup.caption: 1. Count out 40 seeds of five kinds: 16, 10, 8, 4 and 2.

setup.art: A child's hand reaching into a cloth bag without looking.
setup.caption: 2. Mix them in a bag. Without looking, take out 5 survivors.

setup.art: Five seeds of only three kinds in a row, with a notebook showing two kinds crossed out.
setup.caption: 3. Count the kinds that are left. Which kinds were lost?

flow.do: 1. Count out the 40 seeds and mix them in the bag. 2. Explain that a storm will leave only 5 alive. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: This population has five kinds. A storm leaves five survivors, picked by chance. How many of the five kinds will get through? Which kind is most at risk? Why?
flow.kid: There are 40 seeds of 5 kinds. Only 5 will get through. Guess how many kinds are left.
flow.parent: Many children say all five kinds, one of each, because there are five survivors and five kinds.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Narrow Neck. Here you guess how many kinds of seed will pass a bottleneck.

flow.do: 1. Your child takes out 5 seeds without looking. 2. Write which kinds got through. 3. Work out the new population: each survivor has 7 young, so multiply each kind by 8. 4. Put the seeds back and try twice more.
flow.say: Take out five without looking. Which kinds got through? Each survivor makes eight in the new population. Write how many of each kind there are now.
flow.kid: Take out 5 seeds without looking. Write the kinds. Multiply each by 8. Try 3 times.
flow.parent: Most tries leave 3 kinds, and some leave 2 or 4. The rarest kind, with 2 seeds, gets through in only about 1 try in 4. The new population is 40 again, but the lost kinds are gone. Take the first seed your fingers touch each time, so size plays no part.
flow.context: In this step of the Narrow Neck you take 5 survivors and work out the population that grows from them.

flow.do: 1. Compare the three tries. 2. Tell your child about the northern elephant seals. 3. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Hunters left about twenty elephant seals. Now there are over two hundred thousand. What do you think their DNA looks like today?
flow.kid: About 20 seals were left alive. Now there are 200,000. What was lost for good?

check.q: A population falls to 5 and grows back to 40. What has changed for good?
options: Some gene versions are gone
Nothing, the number is the same
Every member is now stronger
check.why: The number recovered, but the 40 all descend from 5 survivors, who carried only some of the versions. If you chose 'nothing', count the kinds in your new population. If you chose 'stronger', remember that the survivors were picked by chance, and not for strength.

flow.parent: The seals look healthy and their numbers are large. The loss shows only in their DNA, and it could matter if a new disease arrives.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Narrow Neck. Here you compare your tries with a real bottleneck.

activities.title: The Black Tigers of Similipal: three explanations and four clues
activities.context: In the Similipal forest in Odisha, many tigers have wide black stripes that nearly cover the orange. Wild tigers elsewhere do not. In this activity you weigh three explanations against four real clues.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
a map of India, in an atlas or on a phone

activities.record: Three columns headed Selection, Chance in a small group, and Gene flow. Under each, a tick or a cross for each clue.

setup.art: A phone map of India with a finger pointing at northern Odisha.
setup.caption: 1. Find Similipal in the north of Odisha.

setup.art: A notebook page with three columns headed Selection, Chance and Gene flow.
setup.caption: 2. Write the three explanations as three columns.

setup.art: The same page with ticks and crosses in four rows under the three headings.
setup.caption: 3. For each clue, mark which explanations it fits.

flow.do: 1. Find Similipal on the map. 2. Describe the black tigers. 3. Read out the three explanations and ask which your child thinks is right, and why.
flow.say: Here are three explanations. One: the dark coat helps tigers there. Two: chance made it common in a small group. Three: dark tigers walked in from elsewhere. Which do you pick, and why?
flow.kid: Why are black tigers common in one forest? Pick one of three explanations. Say why.
flow.parent: The black tigers are not a separate kind. They have the same stripes as other tigers, but much wider, so that the stripes run together.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Black Tigers of Similipal. Here you pick the explanation you think is right.

flow.do: 1. Read the four clues below, one at a time. 2. After each clue, your child marks a tick or a cross under each explanation.
flow.say: Clue one. Similipal's tigers are few, and far from other tiger forests. Clue two. Among 395 wild tigers from other forests, nobody had the wide-stripe version. Which explanations do these fit?
flow.kid: Listen to each clue. Put a tick or a cross under each explanation.
flow.parent: Clue three: the DNA of Similipal's tigers has little variety, which is a sign of a small group cut off for a long time. Clue four: the scientists looked for signs that the dark version had been favoured by selection, and found no clear sign. Clue two rules out gene flow from elsewhere. Clues one and three are what chance in a small group needs. Clue four weakens selection, though a sample of 12 tigers cannot rule out a small advantage.
flow.context: In this step of the Black Tigers of Similipal you test three explanations against four clues.

flow.do: 1. Count the ticks. 2. Ask which explanation fits best now. 3. Ask what new evidence could change the answer.
flow.say: Which explanation fits the clues best? What would you need to find to show that the dark coat really does help?
flow.kid: Which explanation has the most ticks? What could change your mind?

check.q: What evidence would show that a dark coat helps tigers in one forest?
options: Dark tigers there raise more cubs than others
Dark tigers are common there
Dark tigers look well hidden to us
check.why: Selection means leaving more young because of a feature. So the evidence must be a count of cubs raised or tigers surviving. Being common is not evidence, because chance can make a version common too. Looking hidden to a person is a guess about what a deer sees.

flow.parent: Vinay Sagar, Uma Ramakrishnan and their team published this work in 2021. They concluded that drift and inbreeding in a small, cut-off population can explain the black tigers.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Black Tigers of Similipal. Here you decide which explanation fits the clues.

activities.title: Three Grasses in One Chapati: a new species in one step
activities.context: The wheat in atta has the chromosomes of three different wild grasses. In this activity paper strips stand for chromosomes. You find out why a hybrid plant has no seeds, and how doubled chromosomes turn a hybrid into a new species.

materials.item: paper in two colours, or newspaper and plain paper
scissors
a pencil and a plate to stand for one cell

activities.safety: Use child-safe scissors, or let a grown-up cut the strips.
activities.record: Three drawings of the plate: the hybrid, the doubled plant, and the cross back to a parent. Under each, write how many strips have no partner.

setup.art: Paper strips on a table: long and short strips in red, long and short strips in blue.
setup.caption: 1. Cut long and short strips in two colours.

setup.art: A plate holding one long red, one short red, one long blue and one short blue strip, none paired.
setup.caption: 2. Make the hybrid. Try to give every strip an exact partner.

setup.art: The plate now holding two of each strip, laid in four neat pairs.
setup.caption: 3. Double every strip. Try again.

flow.do: 1. Cut 4 long and 4 short strips in red, and the same in blue. 2. Lay out Grass A: 2 long red and 2 short red. 3. Lay out Grass B: 2 long blue and 2 short blue. 4. Explain the pairing rule in the note below.
flow.say: Each strip is a chromosome. In Grass A, every strip has an exact partner, the same colour and length. Is that true in Grass B too?
flow.kid: Cut the strips. Make Grass A in red and Grass B in blue. Does every strip have a partner?
flow.parent: The pairing rule: to make pollen or an egg cell, a plant lines up each chromosome with an exact partner and sends one of each pair into the new cell. So a pollen grain of Grass A carries 1 long red and 1 short red. A strip with no partner goes to one side or the other by chance.
flow.context: This is the first step of Three Grasses in One Chapati. Here you make the paper chromosomes of two grass species.

flow.do: 1. Make the hybrid on the plate: 1 long red and 1 short red from Grass A, 1 long blue and 1 short blue from Grass B. 2. Ask your child to pair every strip with an exact partner. 3. Ask what this means for the hybrid's pollen.
flow.say: This is the hybrid seedling. Pair every strip with one of the same colour and length. Can you? What will happen when this plant tries to make pollen?
flow.kid: Make the hybrid: one of each strip. Try to pair them. How many have no partner?
flow.parent: No strip has a partner. The four strips are shared out by chance, so most pollen and egg cells miss a long or a short. Few or none work, and the hybrid sets almost no seed. A mule is in the same position, with 63 chromosomes.
flow.context: In this step of Three Grasses in One Chapati you find out why a hybrid of two species has few or no seeds.

flow.do: 1. Double the hybrid: add a second copy of every strip. 2. Ask your child to pair the strips now. 3. Then cross the doubled plant back to Grass A: put 1 of each of the four kinds of strip on the plate with 1 long red and 1 short red. Pair again.
flow.say: A cell copied every chromosome and did not divide. Pair the strips now. Then cross this new plant back with Grass A. Which strips are left without partners?
flow.kid: Double every strip and pair them. Then cross back with Grass A. Which strips have no partner?

check.q: A hybrid plant doubles all the chromosomes. Why is the new plant a new species?
options: They breed with their own kind but not with either parent
They are bigger than the parents
They grow in a new place
check.why: After doubling, every chromosome has a partner, so the plant makes working pollen and eggs. But young from a cross back to a parent have unpartnered chromosomes again. If you chose 'bigger', that is often true of such plants, but size does not make a species. A barrier to breeding does.

flow.parent: After doubling, all 8 strips pair. In the cross back, the 2 blue strips have no partners, so those young set little seed. Now the real numbers. A farmed wheat with 28 chromosomes gives 14. A wild goat grass with 14 gives 7. Their hybrid has 21, and doubling gives 42, which is bread wheat. This happened about 9,000 years ago. The farmed wheat with 28 was made the same way, from two wild grasses, long before.
flow.context: This is the last step of Three Grasses in One Chapati. Here you double the chromosomes and find out why the new plant is a new species.

activities.title: The Founders' Boat: can a rare kind become common on an island?
activities.context: The founder effect happens when a few members start a new population. In this activity 50 beans are a mainland population, and 2 of them are a rare speckled kind. Five beans at a time sail off to start an island.

materials.item: pale beans of one kind, such as white karamani or kabuli chana
a marker or sketch pen, to put dots all over 2 of the beans
a deep bowl or dabba and a cloth to cover it
a notebook and a pencil

activities.record: Ten rows, one for each boat. Write how many speckled beans were on board.

setup.art: A bowl of fifty pale beans with two speckled beans visible among them.
setup.caption: 1. Put 48 plain beans and 2 speckled beans in the bowl.

setup.art: A child with eyes shut lifting five beans out of a cloth-covered bowl and placing them in a small paper boat.
setup.caption: 2. With eyes shut, take 5 founders for the boat.

setup.art: A notebook page with ten rows, most reading 0 and two reading 1.
setup.caption: 3. Write how many are speckled. Put them back. Send 10 boats.

flow.do: 1. Dot 2 beans all over and mix them with 48 plain beans. 2. Work out the speckled share on the mainland together. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Two beans in fifty are speckled. Five founders will sail to an empty island. Out of ten boats, how many will carry a speckled bean? Why?
flow.kid: 2 beans in 50 are speckled. Guess how many boats out of 10 will carry one.
flow.parent: The speckled share on the mainland is 2 out of 50, which is 4 in every 100.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Founders' Boat. Here you guess how often a rare kind will be among five founders.

flow.do: 1. Cover the bowl and stir. 2. Your child takes 5 beans with eyes shut. 3. Write how many are speckled. 4. Put them back. 5. Send 10 boats.
flow.say: Stir, shut your eyes and take five founders. Is a speckled bean on board? Write the number and put them back.
flow.kid: Take 5 beans with eyes shut. Write how many are speckled. Put them back. Send 10 boats.
flow.parent: Expect a speckled bean on about 2 boats in 10. Getting none in 10 boats happens about 1 time in 8, and is a fair result. If that happens, send 10 more.
flow.context: In this step of the Founders' Boat you send ten boats of five founders and look for the rare kind.

flow.do: 1. Pick one boat that carried a speckled bean. 2. Work out the speckled share among those 5 founders. 3. Compare it with the mainland share.
flow.say: On this boat, one founder in five is speckled. Is that more or less than on the mainland? How many times more?
flow.kid: On one boat, 1 founder in 5 is speckled. Compare that with 2 in 50.

check.q: A rare version is common on an island started by five founders. What is the simplest explanation?
options: One founder happened to carry the version
The version helps on islands
The island caused the version
check.why: One in 5 is 20 in every 100, which is five times the mainland share of 4 in 100. No help from the version is needed. If you chose 'helps on islands', that could be true, but it would need evidence that carriers leave more young there.

flow.parent: Most islands get no speckled bean at all, so the rare kind is missing there. A few islands get one, and on those the rare kind starts five times more common. Both results make an island differ from the mainland.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Founders' Boat. Here you compare the island's share of the rare kind with the mainland's.

activities.title: Which Bowl? What one bean can tell you about a group
activities.context: Human populations differ in the shares of gene versions, and not in having different genes. In this activity three bowls hold dark and pale beans in slightly different shares. You are shown one bean and try to say which bowl the bean came from.

materials.item: dark beans and pale beans from the Lucky Tumbler Test
bowls of the same kind, labelled 1, 2 and 3 underneath
a notebook and a pencil

activities.record: Twelve rows. In each row write the bean's colour, your guess of the bowl and whether you were right.

setup.art: Three identical steel bowls, each holding a mix of dark and pale beans that looks almost the same.
setup.caption: 1. Bowl 1: 10 dark and 10 pale. Bowl 2: 12 dark and 8 pale. Bowl 3: 8 dark and 12 pale.

setup.art: A grown-up holding up one bean in a closed fist behind three bowls while a child looks at the bean and thinks.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up takes one bean from a bowl in secret and shows the bean.

setup.art: A notebook page with twelve rows of guesses, about four ticked.
setup.caption: 3. Guess the bowl. Do this 12 times and count your right guesses.

flow.do: 1. Fill the three bowls as in the first picture. 2. Let your child look at all three and learn the numbers. 3. Ask for a guess: out of 12 tries, how many will they get right, and why?
flow.say: The three bowls differ, and you know how. I will show you one bean. You say which bowl. How many will you get right out of twelve? Why?
flow.kid: Look at the three bowls. Guess how many you will get right out of 12.
flow.parent: Guessing with no information at all gives about 4 right out of 12.
flow.context: This is the first step of Which Bowl? Here you learn the three bowls and guess how well you will do.

flow.do: 1. Your child turns away. 2. Pick a bowl in an order they cannot predict, and take one bean without looking. 3. Show the bean. Your child names the bowl. 4. Tell them the answer and put the bean back. 5. Do this 12 times.
flow.say: Here is one bean. Which bowl did this bean come from? Tell me why you chose that bowl.
flow.kid: Look at the bean. Say which bowl. Write if you were right. Do it 12 times.
flow.parent: The best plan is to say bowl 2 for a dark bean and bowl 3 for a pale one. Even that is right only about 5 times in 12. Most children score between 3 and 7.
flow.context: In this step of Which Bowl? you try to name the bowl from a single bean.

flow.do: 1. Count the right guesses. 2. Ask the questions below. 3. Explain the link to human populations in the note.
flow.say: The bowls really are different. So why is one bean so little help? What does that tell us about one person and their group?
flow.kid: Count your right guesses. Why is one bean so little help?

check.q: Two groups differ only in the shares of gene versions. What can one member's version tell you?
options: Very little about which group they are from
Exactly which group they are from
That the groups are different species
check.why: Both versions are found in both groups, so one member could come from either. If you chose 'exactly', look at your score in Which Bowl? Groups that differ only in shares, and that still exchange members, are one species.

flow.parent: Human populations are like these bowls, for nearly every gene. About 85 parts in 100 of human genetic variety is found inside any one population. With many thousands of DNA letters read together, a scientist can usually tell where most of a person's ancestors lived. That works by adding up many small differences in shares. It does not mean any sharp line exists.
flow.context: This is the last step of Which Bowl? Here you think about what one member can tell you about a group.

projects.title: Sixteen Islands: repeat a famous fly experiment with beans
projects.context: In 1956 Peter Buri followed 107 small populations of fruit flies for 19 generations. In this three-day project you run 16 islands of beans in the same way, draw the same kind of chart, and compare your result with his.

materials.item: the dark and pale beans and the steel tumbler from the Lucky Tumbler Test
squared paper or a notebook, a pencil and a ruler

projects.safety: Dry beans are a choking risk for children under three.

schedule.what: Run 6 islands of 8 beans for 10 rounds each, as in the Lucky Tumbler Test. Write the final number of dark beans for each.
Run 6 more islands. Add the four islands from the Lucky Tumbler Test, to make 16 in all.
Draw a bar chart of the 16 final counts. Compare it with Buri's flies and explain it to someone.

projects.record: A list of 16 final counts, and a bar chart with five bars: islands that ended with 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8 dark beans.

setup.art: A child running the tumbler test at a table, with a notebook list of island numbers and final counts.
setup.caption: 1. Run 6 islands a day. Write each island's final dark count.

setup.art: A bar chart on squared paper with tall bars at 0 and 8 and short bars at 2, 4 and 6.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a bar for each final count: 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8.

setup.art: A child showing the bar chart to a grandmother and pointing at the two tall end bars.
setup.caption: 3. Explain your chart to someone at home.

flow.do: 1. Run 6 islands, each from 4 dark and 4 pale, for 10 rounds. 2. Write only the final dark count for each. 3. Before starting, your child guesses what the chart of all 16 will look like.
flow.say: Every island starts at four dark. If we ran sixteen islands, what would a chart of their final counts look like? Draw your guess first.
flow.kid: Guess what the chart of 16 islands will look like. Then run 6 islands for 10 rounds each.
flow.parent: Many children draw one tall bar in the middle, at 4. Keep the drawing. An island that reaches 0 or 8 can stop early, which saves time.
flow.context: This is day 1 of Sixteen Islands. Here you guess the shape of the final chart and run the first six islands.

flow.do: 1. Run 6 more islands in the same way. 2. Copy in the final counts of Islands A to D from the Lucky Tumbler Test. 3. Check that the list has 16 counts.
flow.say: Six more islands today. Then we add the four from the Lucky Tumbler Test. That makes sixteen.
flow.kid: Run 6 more islands. Add your four from the Lucky Tumbler Test. You need 16 counts.
flow.parent: If your child did not keep the Lucky Tumbler results, run 4 more islands on day 3.
flow.context: This is day 2 of Sixteen Islands. Here you finish the sixteen islands.

flow.do: 1. Draw a bar chart: final dark counts 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8 along the bottom, number of islands up the side. 2. Compare the chart with the guess from day 1. 3. Read the note about Buri's flies together. 4. Your child explains the chart to someone at home.
flow.say: Where are the tall bars? Is that what you drew on day one? Now explain to someone why the islands ended up at the two ends.
flow.kid: Draw the bar chart. Compare it with your guess. Explain it to someone at home.

ask.q: Why are the tall bars at the two ends, and not in the middle?
good: An island can leave the middle but cannot leave an end.
Once a colour is lost, the count is stuck at 0 or 8.

flow.parent: Expect about 12 of 16 islands at 0 or 8, split roughly evenly between the two, and about 4 still mixed. Buri's chart had the same shape. His 107 bottles each held 16 flies, and began with two gene versions in equal shares. After 19 generations more than half had lost one version or the other, about as many one way as the other. His bottles held more parents than your islands, so they drifted more slowly.
flow.context: This is day 3 of Sixteen Islands. Here you chart the sixteen islands and compare them with a real experiment on flies.

challenges.title: The Wide Crossing: build a road that animals can walk under
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. A highway through a forest stops gene flow unless animals can cross. On National Highway 44 in the Pench tiger forests, the road is raised on pillars so that animals walk beneath. Here you build a model of such a road from paper.
challenges.problem: Build a raised road from newspaper and tape. It must leave a gap underneath that is 30 centimetres wide and 12 centimetres high, with no pillar inside the gap. It must hold a full 500 millilitre water bottle in the middle for 10 seconds.
constraints: Use only 6 sheets of newspaper and 1 metre of tape.
The gap for animals must be 30 centimetres wide and 12 centimetres high, with nothing standing in it.
The road must be at least 10 centimetres wide, so the bottle can lie on it.
The bottle lies on its side at the middle of the road for 10 seconds.
materials: a plastic water bottle of 500 millilitres, full, with the cap on tight
a steel tumbler about 10 centimetres tall, to stand for an elephant walking under
general: Roll sheets of newspaper into tight tubes and tape them. Tubes make strong pillars and strong beams.
Fold a sheet into a long box or a zigzag to make a stiff road deck.
Put pillars at both ends of the gap and tape them to a paper base so they cannot spread.
creative: Make an arch of bent tubes under the road, with the feet of the arch outside the gap.
Make triangles of tubes above the road and hang the deck from them.
Use two tube beams side by side with a folded zigzag sheet between them, like the inside of a carton.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own crossing. Draw it, build it and test it with the bottle. Then ask a harder question: which animals would use your gap, and which would stay away? What would you change for them?

setup.art: Tight newspaper tubes taped as pillars at each end of a marked 30 centimetre gap on the floor, with a ruler lying across.
setup.caption: 1. Mark a gap 30 centimetres wide. Build pillars outside it.

setup.art: A folded newspaper deck resting on tube beams across the gap, 12 centimetres above the floor, with a steel tumbler standing underneath.
setup.caption: 2. Lay the road across. Check that the tumbler fits under it.

setup.art: A child gently laying a water bottle on its side at the middle of the paper road while counting.
setup.caption: 3. Lay the full bottle in the middle. Count to 10.

flow.do: 1. Mark the 30 centimetre gap on the floor with two pencils. 2. Stand the tumbler in it. 3. Tell your child about the highway through Pench, and ask what a good crossing needs.
flow.say: A road cuts a forest in two. Tigers and deer must get across to find mates. What does a crossing need, for the lorries and for the animals?
flow.kid: A road cuts a forest in two. What does a good animal crossing need?
flow.parent: Camera traps under the Pench crossings photographed 18 kinds of wild animals in 2019, including 11 different tigers. The crossings there are between 50 and 750 metres wide.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Wide Crossing challenge. Here you think about what a road needs so that animals can still cross.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws a design. 2. They build it with the newspaper and tape. 3. They check the gap with the ruler and the tumbler.
flow.say: Draw your road first, then build it. Check the gap: thirty wide, twelve high, and nothing standing in it.
flow.kid: Draw your road. Build it. Check the gap with the ruler and the tumbler.
flow.parent: A flat sheet of newspaper sags at once. Let your child find that out, then ask which shapes are stiffer than a flat sheet. A grown-up helps with the scissors.
flow.context: In this step of the Wide Crossing challenge you build your first raised road.

flow.do: 1. Lay the full bottle on its side at the middle of the road. 2. Count to 10. 3. If the road sags or falls, find the part that gave way and rebuild it. 4. Test again.
flow.say: Lay the bottle in the middle and count to ten. Which part bent first? Change that part and test again.
flow.kid: Lay the bottle on the road. Count to 10. Fix the part that bent. Test again.
flow.parent: The first road often folds in the middle or its pillars lean outwards. Tubes rolled tighter, a deeper fold in the deck and pillars taped to a base usually fix it.
flow.context: In this step of the Wide Crossing challenge you test the road with a full bottle and improve it.

flow.do: 1. Look at the finished crossing from the height of the tumbler. 2. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Your road holds the lorry. Now think like a deer. Would you walk under it? What about a frog, or a monkey who lives in treetops?
flow.kid: Your road works. Would a deer walk under it? Would a frog? Would a monkey?

check.q: A road is raised so that animals can walk beneath. Why does this matter for the animals' genes?
options: Animals can reach mates on the other side
The animals get more exercise
The road becomes shorter
check.why: An animal who crosses and has young carries gene versions to the other side. That is gene flow, and it keeps the two halves of the forest one population. Without it, each half is a smaller group, and smaller groups lose variety faster by drift.

flow.parent: Good answers notice that different animals need different crossings. Shy animals want a wide, quiet gap. Frogs need damp ground. Tree-living monkeys and squirrels need a bridge of ropes or branches above the road.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Wide Crossing challenge. Here you think about which animals would use your crossing.

items.p: What is genetic drift?
opts: A change in shares caused by chance
A change caused by a useful feature
Animals moving to a new place
items.why: Drift is change by chance alone. A useful feature spreading is natural selection, moving is gene flow, and a copying mistake is a mutation.

items.p: When every member of a population has the same gene version, that version is said to be ____.
items.why: A fixed version has a share of the whole population. The other versions of that gene are lost.

items.p: True or false: in genetic drift, the version that spreads is always the most useful one.
items.why: False. In drift, which version spreads is decided by chance. A useless version can spread, and a useful one can be lost.

items.p: In which population does chance change the shares fastest?
items.why: The smaller the group, the bigger the part each lucky or unlucky member plays. In large groups, luck nearly cancels out.

items.p: An island of 8 beans became all pale, though nobody chose beans by colour. Explain how.
items.a: In each round, the beans that had young were a small sample picked by chance. By luck, more pale beans were left in some rounds. Each round started from the new numbers, so the changes added up. When dark reached zero, no dark bean was left to have young.
items.why: A strong answer says three things: small samples differ from the whole, the changes add up, and a lost colour cannot return.

items.p: Put these populations in order, from fastest drift to slowest.
a: A million bacteria in a drop of water
items.why: Drift is fastest in the smallest group and slowest in the largest.
items: 20,000 crows in a city
10 tigers in a small forest
A million bacteria in a drop of water
500 deer in a park

items.p: Match each word to its meaning.
items.why: These five words name what chance and movement do to the shares of gene versions.
pairs: a population is cut to a few survivors
a few members start a new population
no member has the version any more

items.p: True or false: after a bottleneck, the lost gene versions come back once the numbers recover.
items.why: False. The new population descends only from the survivors. A lost version can return only by a new mutation or with a migrant.

items.p: Forty seeds of five kinds pass a bottleneck of five survivors. Which kind is most likely to be lost?
items.why: With only 2 seeds among 40, the rarest kind is seldom among 5 picked by chance. Size and colour play no part when the picking is blind.

items.p: Two islands of 8 beans both start with 4 dark. Draw a line chart of how their dark counts might change.
items.a: Two wobbly lines that both start at 4 and go different ways. A line that reaches 0 or 8 stays flat from there on.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the lines wandering differently, and shows that a line cannot leave 0 or 8.
items.art: A blank chart with rounds 0 to 10 along the bottom and dark beans 0 to 8 up the side.

items.p: Sort these cases: was the change caused by chance, or by natural selection?
items.why: In selection the feature itself changes who has young. In drift the feature makes no difference, and the group is small.
items: An island of 8 beans goes all dark in a blind draw
Chance
Pale beans are caught first on a dark cloth
Natural selection
Seals descended from 20 survivors have little variety
Chance
Bacteria that survive a medicine multiply
Natural selection
Bent tails are common where three cats began a population
Chance
Finches with deep beaks survive a drought of hard seeds
Natural selection

items.p: Northern elephant seals number over 200,000. Why does their DNA have so little variety?
opts: The sea is the same everywhere
They are all the same age
items.why: Hunting cut the seals to about 20. Those few carried only part of the old variety, and everyone since has inherited from them.

items.p: Why does chance change a group of 40 more slowly than a group of 8?
items.a: In a group of 40, twenty members become parents. A few lucky ones of one colour are balanced by lucky ones of the other colour, so the share moves little. In a group of 8, only four become parents, and one lucky bean moves the share a long way.
items.why: A strong answer compares the size of the sample that becomes the parents, and says that luck cancels out in a big sample.

items.p: Three of these are cases of genetic drift. Which is the odd one out?
opts: Black tigers common in one small forest
Fly bottles that each lose a gene version
Deeper finch beaks after a drought
A rare illness common on a small island
items.why: Deep beaks cracked the hard seeds, so those finches survived. That is natural selection. In the other three, chance in a small group did the work.

items.p: A feature is found in every animal of one herd. How could you test whether the feature is useful?
items.a: Find a herd where some have the feature and some do not. Count how many young each kind raises, or how many survive, over several years. If those with the feature do no better, the feature may be common by chance.
items.why: A strong answer asks for a count of survival or young, and says that being common is not evidence of being useful.

items.p: What is gene flow?
opts: Genes being lost in a small group
items.why: Gene flow happens when a member moves to another population and has young there. Copying mistakes are mutations, and loss in a small group is drift.

items.p: True or false: a tiger who walks to a new forest but has no cubs there has moved genes.
items.why: False. Gene versions arrive in the new population only when the traveller has young there.

items.p: A strip of forest that joins two larger wild places is called a wildlife ____.
items.why: Animals use a corridor to move between the two places, which keeps gene flow going.

items.p: One island is all dark beans, another all pale. One bean crosses each way every round. What happens to the difference?
items.why: Each traveller brings a colour the island lacked, and that colour is copied there. So the two islands move towards the same shares.

items.p: One migrant is a tiny part of a population. Why can one migrant in each generation still matter so much?
items.a: The migrant may bring a version the population had lost or never had. That version is then passed on and copied. A new migrant arrives in every generation, so the effect adds up. Drift is slow in a large group, so little mixing is needed to balance it.
items.why: A strong answer says that the migrant's version is inherited, and that migrants keep arriving.

items.p: Match each barrier to a real example.
items.why: Each example shows a different way that two groups are kept from having young together.
pairs: Breeding at different times of year

items.p: Sort these barriers: do they act before mating, or after mating?
items.why: Barriers before mating stop the two from meeting or choosing each other. Barriers after mating act on the hybrid young.
items: They breed in different months
Before mating
Their hybrid young cannot have young
After mating
Their songs differ
Before mating
Their hybrid young die early
After mating
A sea lies between them
Before mating
Different insects carry their pollen
Before mating

items.p: Put these steps in order, to show how one species becomes two.
a: A barrier stops the gene flow
Each group changes in different ways
The two groups can no longer breed together
items.why: Gene flow must stop first. Then separate mutations, drift and selection build up differences, until breeding together fails.
items: Each group changes in different ways
The two groups can no longer breed together
One population exchanges genes freely
A barrier stops the gene flow

items.p: A mule has 63 chromosomes. Why can a mule not have young?
opts: An odd number cannot be shared out evenly
63 is too many for any animal
Mules do not live long enough
items.why: To make egg or sperm cells, chromosomes must pair up and separate. With 63, one is always left without a partner, so the cells do not get full sets.

items.p: Draw two forests with a highway between them. Add two different ways for animals to cross.
items.a: For example: the road raised on pillars so animals walk beneath, and a bridge of ropes or branches above the road for monkeys and squirrels. A tunnel for small animals also counts.
items.why: A strong drawing shows crossings for different kinds of animal, and keeps the gap wide enough for shy ones.
items.art: Two blank forest outlines with a straight road between them.

items.p: Similipal's tigers are few and cut off. Two people disagree about bringing in tigers from other forests.
items.a: A strong answer gives evidence for each side. Florida panthers recovered after eight pumas were brought in. But too many outsiders could swamp what is special in the local tigers. It may suggest bringing in a few and watching the results.
items.why: Both worries are real. Most scientists favour a few migrants for a small, inbred population, with careful checking.

views.says: Bring in a few tigers. New gene versions will make the cubs healthier.
Leave them alone. Outsiders will wash away what makes these tigers special.

items.ask: Which person do you agree with more? What evidence does each have? Is there a way to do both?

items.p: True or false: gene flow makes two populations more different from each other.
items.why: False. Gene flow carries each population's versions into the other, so they become more alike. Drift and separate selection make them more different.

items.p: Eight pumas from Texas were released among the last Florida panthers. What did the pumas bring?
opts: Gene versions the panthers had lost
items.why: The small panther population had lost much of its variety through drift and inbreeding. The pumas' young carried versions from a larger population.

items.p: A new highway with no crossings cuts a forest in two. Predict what happens to the animals' genes over 100 years.
items.a: Each half is now a smaller population, so drift is faster. Each side loses some gene versions, and the two sides lose different ones. The two halves become less varied inside and more different from each other. Inbreeding may rise.
items.why: A strong answer says that the halves are smaller, that drift speeds up, and that the two sides grow apart.

items.p: Three of these stop gene flow. Which is the odd one out?
opts: A hot lowland between cool hilltops
items.why: A corridor joins two wild places and lets animals move between them. The other three keep populations apart.

worksheets.title: Doubled Chromosomes, Chance Against Selection, and One Human Species (challenge)

items.p: Bread wheat has 42 chromosomes, in sets of 7. How many sets is that?
items.why: 42 ÷ 7 = 6. The six sets came from three wild grasses, two sets from each.

items.p: Explain why a hybrid of two plant species often sets no seed.
items.a: The hybrid has one set of chromosomes from each parent, and the two sets do not match. To make pollen and eggs, chromosomes must pair with exact partners. With no partners, they are shared out unevenly, so most pollen and egg cells lack some instructions.
items.why: A strong answer says that the chromosomes cannot pair, and links pairing to making working pollen and eggs.

items.p: A hybrid has four chromosomes: long red, short red, long blue, short blue. Draw the cell after doubling, with partners paired.
items.a: Eight strips in four pairs: two long red together, two short red together, two long blue together, two short blue together.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that after doubling every chromosome has an exact partner.
items.art: A large blank circle standing for one cell.

items.p: True or false: chromosome doubling can make a new plant species in a single generation.
items.why: True. The doubled plant can breed with others like themself, but young from crosses back to either parent have unpartnered chromosomes.

items.p: A wheat's egg cell carries 14 chromosomes. A goat grass's pollen carries 7. How many does their hybrid have?
items.why: 14 + 7 = 21. The hybrid has 21, which cannot pair evenly. Doubling gives 42, the number in bread wheat.

items.p: Motoo Kimura's idea that most DNA changes spread by chance is called the ____ theory.
items.why: A neutral change makes no difference to survival, so only chance decides whether it spreads.

items.p: Two scientists disagree about what has shaped most of the DNA differences between species.
items.a: A strong answer gives evidence for each. Changes that leave a protein the same pile up fastest, which fits chance. But beaks and wings clearly fit their uses, which only selection explains. It may say each is right about a different kind of change.
items.why: Both are partly right. Selection explains features that fit a way of life. For DNA letters, scientists still argue over the shares of chance and selection.

views.says: Populations are large, so chance cancels out. Selection decides nearly everything.
Most DNA changes make no difference. They spread or vanish by chance.

items.ask: Which scientist do you find more convincing? What evidence does each have? Could both be right about different things?

items.p: Tomoko Ohta studied very slightly harmful gene versions. In which population can such a version spread?
opts: A small one, where drift is strong
A huge one, where selection is strong
items.why: Weak selection removes a slightly harmful version from a large population. In a small population chance is stronger than such weak selection.

items.p: Black tigers are common in one small forest and absent elsewhere. Give two clues that point to chance rather than selection.
items.a: Any two: the population is small and cut off, which is where drift is fastest. Their DNA has little variety, a sign of a small isolated group. Scientists found no clear sign that the dark version was favoured. No wild tigers elsewhere carry the version.
items.why: A strong answer uses the size and isolation of the population, and notes that nobody has shown dark tigers leaving more cubs.

items.p: Sort these by what they do to a population.
items.why: Mutation makes new versions. Selection and drift change the shares within one population. Gene flow moves versions between populations.
items: A DNA letter is miscopied
Mutation
Bacteria that survive a medicine multiply
Natural selection
A version vanishes from a group of 8 by luck
Genetic drift
Pollen blows in from the next field
Gene flow
A cell's chromosomes double
Mutation
A young tiger fathers cubs in a new forest
Gene flow
Twenty survivors refound a population
Genetic drift
Camouflaged prey are caught less often
Natural selection

items.p: True or false: most human genetic variety can be found within any one population.
items.why: True. About 85 parts in 100 of human variety is inside any one population. Human groups differ in shares of versions, and not in kind.

items.p: Three bowls hold dark and pale beans in slightly different shares. Why can one bean not tell you the bowl?
items.a: Every bowl holds both colours. A dark bean is a little more likely to come from the bowl with more dark beans, but could easily come from any of the three. The bowls differ in shares, and one bean cannot show a share.
items.why: A strong answer says that both colours are in every bowl, and that a share is a fact about a group and not about one member.

items.p: Apple flies and hawthorn flies live in the same countryside. What mostly keeps them apart?
opts: Their fruits ripen at different times
items.why: The flies mate on the fruit they use, and apples ripen weeks before hawthorn fruit. So most apple flies have finished mating before hawthorn flies come out.

items.p: Put the history of bread wheat in order.
a: Their hybrid's chromosomes double, giving a wheat with 28
That wheat crosses with a wild goat grass
The new hybrid's chromosomes double, giving 42
items.why: Bread wheat was made by crossing and doubling twice. Each doubling gave a plant that could set seed with their own kind.
items: That wheat crosses with a wild goat grass
Two wild grasses cross
The new hybrid's chromosomes double, giving 42
Their hybrid's chromosomes double, giving a wheat with 28

items.p: Is a species something real in nature, or a label people use? Give one piece of evidence for each side.
items.a: Real: a firefly answers only the flashes of her own kind, and a mule cannot have young, so nature itself keeps some groups apart. A label: apple flies and hawthorn flies are part of the way to being two species, and scientists disagree about where to draw such lines.
items.why: A strong answer gives evidence for both sides. Species split slowly, so some lines are sharp and some are not.

quiz.p: Beans are drawn blind, and neither colour is better. One colour still takes over. What is this called?
quiz.why: Change in shares by chance alone is genetic drift. Choosing natural selection would mean that one colour helped beans survive, and here neither did.

quiz.p: Why does chance change a population of 8 faster than a population of 800?
opts: A small sample often differs from the whole
Large groups do not have genes
quiz.why: With few parents, a little luck moves the shares a long way. With many parents, lucky and unlucky members nearly cancel out.

quiz.p: True or false: a version lost by drift comes back by itself in a few generations.
quiz.why: False. Once no member carries a version, nobody can pass it on. Only a new mutation or a migrant can bring it back.

quiz.p: A population is cut to 20 survivors and grows back to thousands. What is this event called?
quiz.why: A bottleneck squeezes a population through a few survivors. Their descendants carry only the versions those few had.

quiz.p: Three cats start an island population. One has a bent tail. Bent tails become common. What is the simplest cause?
opts: The cats wished for bent tails
quiz.why: With three founders, one cat's version starts at a large share. No advantage is needed. Saying the bend helps would need evidence that bent-tailed cats raise more kittens.

quiz.p: What does gene flow do to two populations?
quiz.why: Travellers who breed carry each population's versions into the other. Choosing 'more different' describes drift, which gene flow works against.

quiz.p: Roughly how many breeding migrants per generation keep two populations from drifting far apart?
quiz.why: About one migrant per generation is enough in the mathematics. Wildlife managers aim for between 1 and 10, because real populations are messier.

quiz.p: True or false: for two populations to become two species, gene flow between them must nearly stop.
quiz.why: True. While versions keep passing between them, the two change together. Differences that block breeding build up only when they are apart.

quiz.p: Which of these is a barrier that acts after two animals have mated?
quiz.why: A mule is healthy but cannot breed, so no genes pass on. The other three stop the two from meeting or choosing each other in the first place.

quiz.p: How can a new plant species form in a single generation?
opts: A seed lands on an island
quiz.why: Doubling gives every chromosome a partner, so the plant sets seed with their own kind but not with either parent. Landing on an island starts a split that takes thousands of generations.

quiz.p: A feature is common in one population. What would show that the feature is useful?
opts: Members with the feature raise more young
Nearly every member has the feature
quiz.why: Useful means leaving more young because of the feature, and that can be counted. Being common is not enough, because chance can make a feature common too.

quiz.p: Human populations differ mainly in what?
quiz.why: All humans have the same genes, in versions found nearly everywhere. Populations differ in how common each version is, because gene flow has always joined them.

applications: Wildlife managers plan forest corridors and road crossings so that tigers, elephants and smaller animals can keep exchanging genes.
Managers move a few animals between cut-off populations to restore lost variety. Two tigresses were moved from Maharashtra to Similipal in late 2024 for this reason.
Zoos keep records of every animal's parents and choose mates who are not close relatives. This slows the loss of gene versions in small zoo populations.
Doctors use the founder effect to know which inherited illnesses to look for first in a community that grew from few founders.
Seed banks store many varieties of rice, ragi and wheat. A crop grown from very few parent plants has passed a bottleneck, and one disease can then harm every plant.
Plant breeders double chromosomes on purpose to make new crops. Triticale, a cross of wheat and rye, was made this way.
Scientists count DNA differences that spread by chance to estimate how long ago two species separated. This is the molecular clock.

open_questions.q: How much of the difference between species came by chance, and how much by selection?
open_questions.why_open: For DNA letters, scientists still disagree. Kimura and Ohta showed that chance must do a great deal. Some studies of whole genomes suggest that selection touches more of the DNA than their theories allow.

open_questions.q: How many gene changes does it take to make two populations unable to breed together?
open_questions.why_open: In a few cases, such as some fruit flies, scientists have found single genes that make hybrids unable to breed. In most species nobody knows the number, or whether it is usually a few genes or many.

open_questions.q: How often do animals split into two species with no barrier in space?
open_questions.why_open: Apple maggot flies and some lake fishes suggest that this can happen. It is hard to prove that the two groups were never apart at any time in the past.

open_questions.q: Does the dark coat help the tigers of Similipal at all?
open_questions.why_open: The 2021 study found no clear sign of an advantage, but it could test only 12 wild tigers from Similipal. A small advantage or disadvantage would need many years of counting cubs.

open_questions.q: Do any mutations begin with a quantum jump of a single particle in DNA?
open_questions.why_open: Per-Olov Löwdin proposed this in 1963. Calculations have been made since, but nobody has shown it happening inside a living cell.

maths.problem: After round 2, Island A had 6 dark beans out of 8. The big group had 18 dark beans out of 40. Both started at one half. Which has moved further from one half?
maths.answer: Island A. Its dark share moved by one quarter. The big group's share moved by only one twentieth.
maths.explain: 6 out of 8 is 6 ÷ 8 = 0.75. One half is 0.5, so the island moved by 0.25. 18 out of 40 is 18 ÷ 40 = 0.45, so the big group moved by 0.05. The island moved five times as far.
maths.context: This is about the Lucky Tumbler Test. There you take out half the beans with eyes shut in every round, on islands of 8 beans and in a group of 40. These are made-up results.

chart.title: Made-up example results: dark beans after round 2

maths.why_maths: The two groups are different sizes, so the counts cannot be compared directly. Turning each count into a share shows which group chance has moved more.

maths.problem: A tumbler holds 4 dark and 4 pale beans. There are 70 different sets of 4 beans you could draw. Exactly 36 of those sets have 2 dark and 2 pale. Is a 2 and 2 draw more or less likely than not?
maths.answer: Very slightly more likely than not: 36 chances in 70, which is just over one half.
maths.explain: Half of 70 is 35. 36 is one more than 35, so the chance is just over one half. 36 ÷ 70 = 0.51 to two places. So in 10 draws you should expect about 5 to be 2 and 2, and about 5 to be something else.
maths.context: This is about Four From Eight. There you draw 4 beans with eyes shut from a tumbler of 4 dark and 4 pale, ten times.
maths.why_maths: Counting all the possible draws tells you what to expect before you try. Then you can judge whether your ten draws were ordinary or unusual.

maths.problem: On the mainland, 2 beans in 50 are speckled. On one island, 1 of the 5 founders is speckled. How many times more common is the speckled kind on the island?
maths.explain: 2 out of 50 is the same share as 4 out of 100. 1 out of 5 is the same share as 20 out of 100. 20 ÷ 4 = 5. So the speckled kind starts 5 times more common on the island.
maths.context: This is about the Founders' Boat. There you draw 5 beans from a bowl of 48 plain beans and 2 speckled ones, to start an island.
maths.why_maths: Writing both shares out of 100 lets you compare a group of 50 with a group of 5. The comparison shows how strongly a few founders can change a share.

maths.problem: A farmed wheat has 28 chromosomes and a wild goat grass has 14. Each parent gives half. How many chromosomes does their hybrid have? How many after doubling? How many sets of 7 is that?
maths.answer: The hybrid has 21. After doubling there are 42, which is 6 sets of 7.
maths.explain: Half of 28 is 14, and half of 14 is 7. 14 + 7 = 21. Doubling gives 21 × 2 = 42. 42 ÷ 7 = 6 sets. An odd number such as 21 cannot be shared into two equal halves, which is why the hybrid needs doubling to set seed.
maths.context: This is about Three Grasses in One Chapati. There paper strips stand for chromosomes, and you find out how doubling makes a new species.
maths.why_maths: Halving, adding and doubling the chromosome numbers shows exactly why the hybrid cannot make even shares, and why the doubled plant can.

maths.problem: In Similipal, 58 of every 100 copies of the stripe gene are the wide-stripe version. A tiger is black only with two such copies. If the copies came together by chance, what share of tigers would be black? Suppose the forest held 30 tigers: about how many would be black?
maths.answer: About one third of the tigers, so about 10 tigers out of 30.
maths.explain: The chance that the first copy is the wide-stripe version is 0.58. The chance that the second is too is also 0.58. For both together, multiply: 0.58 × 0.58 = 0.34 to two places, which is about one third. One third of 30 is 10. The number 30 is made up for this sum. Real tigers do not pair up by chance alone, so the true share may differ.
maths.context: This is about the Black Tigers of Similipal. There you weigh three explanations for the wide black stripes of the tigers in one forest in Odisha.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying the two chances turns a share of gene copies into a prediction about whole tigers. Scientists then compare such a prediction with the tigers they actually see.

maths.problem: About 20 elephant seals were alive in 1892. Suppose the number doubled again and again. How many doublings does it take to pass 200,000?
maths.answer: 14 doublings. After 13 doublings there are 163,840 seals, and after 14 there are 327,680.
maths.explain: Keep doubling: 20, 40, 80, 160, 320, 640, 1,280, 2,560, 5,120, 10,240, 20,480, 40,960, 81,920, 163,840, 327,680. The thirteenth doubling gives 163,840, which is below 200,000. The fourteenth passes it. Thirteen or fourteen doublings in about 130 years is one doubling every 9 or 10 years.
maths.context: This is about the Narrow Neck. There 40 seeds pass through a bottleneck of 5 survivors, as the northern elephant seals passed through about 20.
maths.why_maths: The doubling pattern shows how quickly numbers can recover after a bottleneck. It makes the point that numbers come back fast while lost gene versions do not come back at all.

maths.problem: Of 16 bean islands, 12 ended with one colour lost. Of Peter Buri's 107 fly bottles, 58 ended with one version lost. Which is the bigger share? Give one reason the shares might differ.
maths.answer: The bean islands: 75 in 100, against about 54 in 100 for the flies. Each fly bottle had more parents than a bean island, so the flies drifted more slowly.
maths.explain: 12 ÷ 16 = 0.75, which is 75 in 100. 58 ÷ 107 = 0.54 to two places, which is 54 in 100. A bean island had 4 parents in each round. A fly bottle had 16. Chance moves a larger group more slowly, so fewer bottles had lost a version, even after more generations.
maths.context: This is about Sixteen Islands. There you run 16 islands of 8 beans for 10 rounds each, and compare them with a real experiment on fruit flies. The count of 12 is a made-up result.

chart.title: Made-up example results: where 16 islands ended

maths.why_maths: Turning both results into shares out of 100 lets you compare 16 islands with 107 bottles. The difference between the shares then becomes something to explain.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that chance alone can change a population? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: In the 1930s Ronald Fisher, an English mathematician, argued that chance hardly matters in evolution. Populations are large, he said, so luck cancels out and natural selection decides nearly everything. Sewall Wright, an American biologist, had worked out in 1931 that chance could change the shares of gene versions in small groups. The two agreed on the mathematics. They disagreed about real animals. In 1956 Peter Buri tested the question with fruit flies. He set up 107 bottles. Each held 8 males and 8 females, and each began with two versions of an eye-colour gene in equal shares. In every generation he picked the 16 parents at random. After 19 generations the bottles looked nothing alike. More than half had lost one version or the other. Selection could not explain it, because the same version won in some bottles and lost in others. Later, Motoo Kimura in 1968 and Tomoko Ohta in 1973 showed that much of the change in DNA spreads in this way.
how_we_found_out.who: Sewall Wright, an American biologist. Peter Buri, who ran the fly experiment in the United States. Motoo Kimura and Tomoko Ohta, Japanese biologists.
how_we_found_out.when: 1931 to 1973. The fly experiment was published in 1956.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That chance is too weak to change a population, so every difference between two populations must be there because it helped. Buri's bottles all had the same conditions, and still ended up different.
how_we_found_out.art: Rows of small glass bottles on a laboratory shelf, each with a few fruit flies inside, and a hand writing counts in a ledger.

roots.context: We have learned how chance, mixing and separation change whole populations. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Lucky Tumbler Test, neither colour was better, and nobody looked at colour. Most islands still ended with a single colour, and different islands kept different ones. So a feature can be found in every member of a group without being of any use. Being common shows that a feature spread. It does not show why.
deep_truth.habit: We ask 'what is it for?' about every feature of a living being, and accept the first answer that sounds sensible. That habit treats 'common' as if it meant 'useful'. Some features are common only because of who happened to be the parents, long ago.
deep_truth.evidence: Three of four islands of 8 beans lost a colour within 10 rounds, with no hunter and no advantage. Peter Buri's fly bottles did the same in 1956. In Similipal, wide black stripes became common in a small, cut-off tiger population, and nobody has found that they help.

three.who_am_i: Some of what you are helped your ancestors to live. Some of it is there because of who happened to meet, and which egg and sperm happened to join. Nobody can sort every part of you into one pile or the other.
three.what_is_life: Life changes in two ways at once. Selection keeps what suits the place, and chance keeps whatever happened to be passed on. Mixing then shares both kinds of change around.
three.what_is_this_world: No population is a closed box. Tigers, pollen and people carry gene versions from place to place. Where the carrying stops for long enough, a new species begins.

roots.thread: All living beings come from one beginning. That one line became millions of species in a plain way: populations stopped mixing, and each went on changing separately. So the many kinds of life are one family whose branches lost touch with each other. Inside each species the mixing still goes on, and it shares every new version among the members. Much of that mixing is chosen. A young tiger decides to leave and walk, and a firefly decides which flash to answer.

teachings.link: Species form slowly, as populations stop mixing. So at any moment some groups are part of the way, like the apple flies and the hawthorn flies. The sharp line is in our word more than in the living beings.
