science.text: Chance alone changes the shares of gene versions in a population, and does so fastest in small populations.
In drift, 'chance' means that the cause had nothing to do with the feature. Each death and each birth still had its own causes.
Most of the DNA differences between species spread by chance, and not because they helped.

other_view.who: Richard Dawkins, an English biologist, and others who stress adaptation
other_view.view: They agree that drift changes DNA letters. But they point out that an eye, a wing or a beak is far too complicated and costly to arise by luck. For anything like that, they say, selection is the only explanation we have. So 'what is it for?' remains the right first question about a body, as long as the answer is then tested.

practice.title: Looking without asking why
practice.say: Hold out one hand and look at the lines on your palm. Nobody has ever shown that their exact pattern is for anything. Your pattern is yours because of how your hand folded before you were born. Breathe in slowly and follow one line with your eyes. Breathe out and follow another. Notice whether your mind wants to give each line a reason. Let the reason go, and keep looking. A thing can be here, and be yours, without being for anything.
practice.kid: Hold out one hand. Look at the lines on your palm. Nobody knows of any use for their exact pattern. Breathe in and follow one line. Breathe out and follow another. Just look, without asking why.

ask: Neither colour was better, yet one took over. If you had seen only the end, what would you have believed?
Can something about you matter if it has no use?
How much of you is there for a reason, and how much because of who happened to meet?
If species have no sharp edges, where does one kind of life stop and the next begin?

playtest: The experiments, activities and games were reasoned through step by step for a city flat, and the bean experiments were run many thousands of times as a computer simulation to find what a family should expect. They have not yet been tried by hand at home. The Lucky Tumbler Test (core) needs 80 pale beans of one kind and a marker. The dark and pale beans must feel the same, so do not mix two kinds of bean. In the simulation, about three of four islands of 8 lost a colour within 10 rounds, and all four still had both colours in fewer than 1 home in 100. The group of 40 stayed between 10 and 30 dark beans in about 9 homes in 10 and almost never lost a colour in 5 rounds. The step says what to do if your result is unusual. In the Bridge Test the difference between the islands fell to 4 or less in more than 9 runs in 10. In Four From Eight, exactly 2 dark comes up in about half the draws. In the Narrow Neck, 3 kinds are left in about half the tries, and the rarest kind gets through about 1 time in 4. In the Founders' Boat, a speckled bean is on about 2 boats in 10, and on none of the 10 about 1 time in 8. Three Grasses in One Chapati and the Wide Crossing need scissors and a grown-up nearby. The Wide Crossing was not built: tight newspaper tubes are known to carry far more than a 500 millilitre bottle, but the first attempt may sag. The numbers in the made-up results agree across the experiments, the maths and the worksheets. Real-world facts were checked by web search on 19 Nov 2026: the Similipal tiger study, Buri's flies, the Florida panthers, the elephant seals, Pingelap, the tiger corridors and the highway crossings at Pench, bread wheat and goatsbeard, the snapping shrimps, the apple maggot fly, Lewontin's figure, the 2017 South Asian study, the horse, donkey and mule chromosome numbers, and the 2024 move of two tigresses to Similipal. Not checked from here: the page numbers of the older papers in the sources list, the lengths of two of the films, and whether Arignar Anna Zoological Park currently shows tigers. The three film ids, titles and channels were confirmed through YouTube's public lookup, but the films were not watched: preview them first.
